Furthermore, just as with a lamp, consciousness is likewise so; because it abides depending on the phenomena of craving and attachment, this serves as a metaphor for the essence of consciousness.

Furthermore, just as with an illusion, the locus upon which it depends is likewise so; because the various distinctions of the vessel-world (bhājanaloka) lack a single, real substance, this serves as a metaphor for the vessel.
Furthermore, just as dew, so too is the body; because it abides for only a short time, this is used as a metaphor for the body.

Furthermore, just as a bubble, so too are the objects of enjoyment; because the three factors—the cause, sensation, and perception—are unstable, this is used as a metaphor for the objects of enjoyment.
Furthermore, just as a dream, so too are past phenomena; because they exist only as mental recollections, this serves as a metaphor for past phenomena.
Furthermore, just as lightning, so too are present phenomena; because they do not abide for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), this is used as an analogy for present phenomena.

Furthermore, just as with clouds, so it is with future dharmas; because at the time of the "seed" (bīja), the ālayavijñāna serves as the fundamental seed for all dharmas, this is used as a metaphor for future dharmas.
[The Ten Treasures]: The *Prabhāsa-sūtra* states:

It is precisely because giving (*dāna*) serves as the foot of the first stage that, once the foot of giving is fulfilled, one enters the first stage; and so on, until the foot of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is fulfilled, whereby one enters the tenth stage.

Ban Gu’s *Book of Han* elucidates the nine schools of thought:

First, the Confucian school (*rúlíu*), which accords with the principles of yin and yang, expounds upon moral transformation and education, recounts the governance of the ages of Yao and Shun, and takes the Way of Zhòngní (Confucius) as its primary tenet.

Second, the Daoist tradition (Daoliu): it maintains weakness and cultivates humility, extolling the virtue of Yao and Shun’s yielding of the throne and upholding the modesty and reverence of the *Zhouyi*.
Third, the Yin-Yang tradition (Yinyangliu): it follows the celestial calendar and astronomical phenomena, respectfully receiving the seasonal timing for the people.
Fourth, the Stream of Dharma (*dharmasrotas*): this clarifies the bestowal of official decrees, acting in accordance with ritual regulations.
Fifth, the Stream of Names (*nāmasrotas*): this correctly establishes names and ranks, signifying that affairs are carried out in accordance with words.
Sixth is the School of Mo (Mohism), which pertains to the ancestral sacrifices in the Hall of Pure Brilliance and the nurturing of the aged through the distribution of wisdom.
Seventh is the School of the Vertical and Horizontal (Zongheng), which refers to receiving diplomatic missions and exercising authority in specialized negotiations.

8. The Miscellaneous Stream (Zaliu): This combines the standards of Confucianism and Mohism and incorporates the teachings of the School of Names and Legalism; it understands the grand principles of statecraft and encompasses all matters without exception.
9. The Agricultural Stream (Nongliu): This encourages the cultivation of grain and sericulture, providing a comprehensive exposition on food and wealth.
Miti said: "Among Sima Qian’s six schools of thought, Daoism is foremost;
among Ban Gu’s nine currents of learning, the Confucian tradition is supreme."

these three factors exist simultaneously in a horizontal alignment, each distinct and unrelated, like a line of blazing fire spread out horizontally.
"New Yi" is a metaphor for the three virtues of the present teaching.
The Dharma-body is simultaneously illumination and simultaneously sovereignty.
Although one is designated as three, these three have no separate substance; therefore, they are not horizontal [distinct entities].
Being neither before nor after, it is not sequential.
One is three, like a large dot;
three are one, like fine lines.
It is three yet one, and one yet three.
It cannot be described as one or three, nor can it be conceived as one or three; therefore, it is called "inconceivable.
That which is inconceivable is neither three nor one; it is named the "Secret Treasury," like the worldly letter *i*.
Guyxiang said:

"The scripts of the Western Regions have both old and new forms, just as in this land we have the seal (zhuàn) and clerical (lì) scripts; none fail to regard the seal script as old and the clerical script as new."
An Appendix: The Method of the Separation and Union of Cultivation and Nature [Samsa]. This term means "separation and union.
To reveal that the three points (*bindu*) do not exist as either vertical or horizontal, one must demonstrate the methods of separation and union regarding cultivation and nature.
When the three paths reach delusion, the Dharma of the rational nature is perfectly complete;
when the two causes open toward enlightenment, the phenomena of cultivation are mutually integrated.
When opened, each is distinct as three; when confronted, they together merge into one.
In discussing these three points, I shall tentatively open ten sections:

First, the main text; Second, explaining the names; Third, interpreting the meaning; Fourth, determining the essence; Fifth, indicating the characteristics; Sixth, investigating the intent; Seventh, judging the teaching; Eighth, defining the stage; Ninth, resolving doubts; Tenth, pointing out errors. First, regarding the main text, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"The intrinsic nature of all dharmas is itself empty."
Furthermore, because the bodhisattva practices emptiness, they perceive all phenomena as empty.
The *Awakening of Faith* states:
"Because one knows that the essence of the dharma-nature is devoid of stinginess and greed, one practices the dāna-pāramitā in accordance with it."
The *Bie xing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Separate Practice) by Tiantai states:
"Tracing back to the fundamental basis of this cause and effect, it is precisely the inherent qualities (*xingde*) of the conditions (*yuan*) and the understanding (*liao*).
These inherent qualities have existed from the very beginning; they are not something acquired only now."
It is further said:

"By practicing through these two kinds of skillful means, they gradually increase; starting from a mere hair’s tip, one attains the cultivation of virtue that becomes a great tree with a trunk of several armspan in girth."
Jingxi’s *Famen* (The Gate of Non-duality) states:
"The nature-merit is precisely the realm-of-reality within a single thought-moment.
Within this internal realm-of-reality, the three dharmas are fully present."
"Although the nature is inherently so, it relies upon wisdom to give rise to cultivation.
These are all clear explanations of the relationship between cultivation and nature.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says:
"The dharma of liberation is not nirvāṇa;
the body of the Tathāgata is not nirvāṇa;
and mahāprajñā is also not nirvāṇa."
Zhang’an’s *Xuanlun on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra* explains:
"The text states that even the Dharma-body is 'not,' so how can it be explained as the Great [Nirvāṇa] by means of the three bodies alone?
The text states that even liberation is 'not,' so how can it be explained as Cessation by means of the three liberations alone?"
The text states that even *prajñā* is not [the ultimate]; how then can it be explained as the three wisdoms (*trividya*) alone?
Thus we know that an exclusive explanation is not the intent of this sutra.
Within each of the three virtues, one seeks them individually, yet they are all unobtainable.
"The three dharmas are sought in conjunction, yet they cannot be obtained.
The *Miaoxuan* states: "This wondrous practice, together with the preceding object and wisdom, is one when discussed as three, and three when discussed as one."
Jingxi said: "Furthermore, regarding the correspondence between cultivation and nature, there is both separation and union.
Separation refers to the three aspects each of cultivation and nature; union refers to the two aspects of cultivation and the one aspect of nature."
Yongjia said:
"Among the three within the partial, one must exercise discernment.
First: there is prajñā, but no liberation or dharmakāya."
Second, there is liberation but no prajñā of the dharmakāya;
third, there is the dharmakāya but no prajñā of liberation.
Because one exists while the other does not, they are not complete; because they are not complete, they are not the true nature.
Furthermore, among the three types of partial [attainments], one must make a distinction:
first, there is liberation through prajñā, but no dharma-body;
second, there is the dharma-body through liberation, but no prajñā.
Third, there is the prajñā of the dharmakāya, yet no liberation.
Because two exist and one is absent, it is not perfect; because it is not perfect, it is not the true nature.
Within perfection, these three must be fully present.
First, the non-delusion of the Dharmakāya is Prajñā;
the non-attachment of Prajñā is Vimukti;
the quiescence of Vimukti is the Dharmakāya—two or three instances are thus analogous.
These are all the original texts concerning separation and conjunction.
Second, regarding the clarification of terms: "cultivation" (xiū) refers to establishing practice and advancing toward realization, giving rise to the two causes of the primary and auxiliary;
"nature" (xìng) refers to the fundamental essence itself, which is the single thought-moment of the realm of suchness (jièrú).
Because ordinary beings are deluded, they give rise to the false from the true, like a mirror obscured by dust.
Since the luminous nature of the conditions and the cause inherently exists, it is endowed with the virtues of the rational nature.

Because the practitioner has attained awakening, they turn their back on the defilements and unite with enlightenment; it is like polishing a mirror, whereby the reflections of beauty and ugliness finally appear, and thus there is the virtue achieved through cultivation.
3. Regarding the explanation of the meaning, this concerns the method of separation and combination. Master Nanping once established three meanings to clarify it:
first, "separation" means "respective"; separation refers to the three aspects of cultivation and nature being distinct.
Second, "combination" means "shared"; combination refers to the two aspects of cultivation being one with the single aspect of nature.
Second, "separation" (li) means opening; in terms of nature (xing), it is eternally open.
"Union" (he) means confronting; it is only through confronting cultivation (xiu) that union occurs.

Third, separation is precisely the meaning of "bestowing" (yu); speaking in terms of bestowal, the one nature is fundamentally present within the two cultivations, and the two cultivations are constantly identical with the one nature.

"Integration" (*he*) has the meaning of "exclusion. Although, in principle, [the nature] possesses both the conditions (*yuan*) and the causes (*liao*), when speaking in terms of exclusion, because one has neither generated the resolve nor applied oneself to practice, those natures—the conditions and causes—are designated only as the "direct cause" (*zhengyin*).
Although the two types of cultivation both possess the Dharma-body, because they are illuminated by wisdom, they are termed "revealing causes" (*jñāna-hetu*).
Because they give rise to practice, they are collectively termed "conditional causes" (*pratyaya-hetu*).

Fourth, regarding the essence of these practices: in order to demonstrate the characteristics of the teachings concerning their separation and integration, one must examine the essential nature of the dharmas of cultivation and inherent nature. This is because both the inherent and the cultivated take the three thousand phenomena in their universal aspect as their essence.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"The Suchness of Mind is the essence of the single Dharma-realm, the great universal characteristic Dharma-gate; that is to say, the nature of mind is neither born nor extinguished."
Although the mind is fundamentally true, it fails to realize this and gives rise to delusion.
As the Sūtra says:
"The mind is like a master painter."
"Constructing the various five aggregates, there is nothing within all the worlds that is not constructed from the mind.
Thus, with ignorance as a condition, the phenomena of sentient beings are formed.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Just as a magician perceives the illusory figures he has conjured, so does a bodhisattva regard sentient beings.
It is through the realization of this principle that there is the Buddha-dharma.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"Only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully exhaust the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
These three dharmas, being mutually present within the three thousand [realms], each likewise encompass the hundred worlds.
To realize its fundamental quiescence is termed "inherent principle" (li-jù);
to illuminate the arising of the mind is termed "phenomenal creation" (shi-zào).
Although the cultivated nature (xiū-xìng) are two, the three thousand realms are one in essence.
Therefore, the *Miaole* states:
"Precisely because the principle is one, the cultivation and nature correspond to one another in their separation and union.
Fifth, the demonstration of characteristics; in Guishan’s *Xianxing lu*, the demonstration of the characteristic of separation is as follows:
The "One Family" (Ekakula) doctrine of the cultivation of nature and the ultimate truth corresponds to the first three wondrous aspects of the *Xuanyan* (Profound Meaning).
The objective realm (*viṣaya*) constitutes the three aspects of nature; wisdom (*jñāna*) constitutes the three aspects of wisdom; and practice (*caryā*) constitutes the three aspects of practice.
The stages through which one progresses constitute the various positions.
Upon reaching the first dwelling (bhūmi), it is called the "fruit according to one's portion," which signifies the partial realization of the three dharmas.
If explained in terms of their integration, the nature (prakṛti) is unified as one, and cultivation (bhāvanā) is unified as two.
The three aspects of rationality unified as a single direct cause constitute the quality of the Dharma-body;
the three aspects of wisdom unified as a single revealing cause constitute the quality of Prajñā;
and the three aspects of practice unified as a single conditional cause constitute the quality of Liberation.
Therefore, although there are nine categories when fully enumerated, these nine are merely three; though the three and the nine differ, their underlying principle remains ever one.
Examining this teaching now, its phrasing is coherent and its meaning convenient for explaining the sense of "separation."

Wenhui’s *Shiqian* states: "The object (*viṣaya*) is the rational nature of the three virtues; wisdom is the understanding of the three virtues; and practice is the contemplation of the three virtues.
Furthermore, to clarify the convergence of these meanings, Wenhui’s *Shiqian* says: "'One' refers to nirvāṇa; 'three' refers to the three virtues."

Regarding the meaning of "convenience": since separation and union constitute delusion and awakening, and bestowal and withdrawal must pertain to the stage prior to abiding, once one reaches the First Abode (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), cultivation and nature are unified and no longer divided; how then could one discuss the distinction between bestowal and withdrawal?
The *Zhijiao chao* (Essential Commentary) states:

"As in the ten kinds of threefold dharmas in the *Guangming xuán*, which extract the doctrinal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of cultivation and nature from the sūtras and śāstras, it thus contains both the dual and unified explanations."
As with the three virtues and the Three Jewels, although they represent the ultimate of cultivated virtue, their meaning necessarily encompasses the inherent nature;
as with the three bodies and the three wisdoms, although the texts refer primarily to awakening, their principle necessarily extends to delusion;
and as with the three consciousnesses and the three paths, since these point to phenomena as being identical to principle, cultivation must arise entirely from the inherent nature.
Are these six not each comprised of three aspects—cultivation and nature?
Since the three causes consist of one aspect of nature contrasted with the two aspects of cultivation (wisdom and practice);

so too do the three types of enlightenment, the three Great Vehicles, and the three nirvāṇas consist of one aspect of nature contrasted with the two aspects of cultivation (realizing the principle and giving rise to function).
Are these four not, in fact, the cultivation of two natures as one?
Now, I maintain that the gate of the unity of cultivation and nature fundamentally relies upon the two subtleties of wisdom and practice.

The subtlety regarding the object lies in the principle of delusion; through the mutual granting and taking away of opposites, one discusses their separation and union, whereby the ten kinds of threefold dharmas are revealed.
The three virtues realized by those who have attained the fruit all belong to awakening; yet to abandon the primary text and seek them remotely in other sections is a confusion regarding the wording.
Furthermore, there are two major meanings concerning the "separation and integration" (li-he) of the Shanjia school:

first, regarding the mutual formation of the cultivated and the inherent (xiu-xing), when situated within the inherent nature, the entirety of the cultivated forms the inherent nature, and the inherent nature itself possesses these three [virtues].
When cultivation arises, the entire nature becomes cultivation, and cultivation itself inherently possesses the three [aspects].

Second, regarding the relative relationship between cultivation and nature: "separately" means that both cultivation and nature each possess three [aspects], while "combined" means that cultivation has two and nature has one.

Now, by using three for both cultivation and nature while explaining six for cultivation and three for nature, this conflates the characteristics of mutual correspondence and further confuses the enumeration of the six and nine dharmas; this is contrary to the correct meaning!
3. Jingjue’s *Miscellaneous Compilation* (*Zabian*) states:

"I once wrote a commentary on the *Wenxin diaolong*, in which I cited the *Xuanshan* in detail to annotate it; its general meaning does not differ from that of Gushan, as we both explain that 'separation' and 'sameness' are distinct."
"However, by taking the three—object, wisdom, and practice—and correlating them perfectly with the three virtues, this explanation reconciles their differences.
Thus, the *Zabian* states:
"Among the three bodies, the Dharma-body is easily understood; the Reward-body is Prajñā, and the Response-body is Vimukti."
Among the three kinds of *prajñā*, the true mark (*dharmatā*) is the *dharmakāya*, contemplative observation is *prajñā*, and words and letters are liberation (*vimukti*).
Among the three kinds of liberation, essential purity is the *dharmakāya*, circular purity is *prajñā*, and purity through skillful means is liberation.
This resembles the joining of palms, and is also like the merging of the three strokes of the character for "river" (川).

If one attributes the nature, the virtues, and the conditions of awakening (緣了) to the cultivated, the retributive, and the responsive [bodies], then within the cultivated [body], the Dharma-body would merely join with the nature-as-true-cause (性正因).

This would lose the meaning of "giving and taking away," and furthermore, it would contradict the *Golden Scalpel* (金錍). Therefore, the nature, the conditions, and the awakening are all designated by the same name: "true cause."
Fourth, regarding the South Pavilion’s [treatment of] the severance of union and separation, there are four major points.
First is the "three-in-one.
The *Shiqian* states:
"One refers to Nirvana; the three refer to the Three Virtues.

Regarding the "Two, Three, and Six," there are originally three types in the *Jinpi* (The Golden Scalpel). The three principles are fundamentally pervasive; by realizing the nature, one accomplishes cultivation, and the three cultivated virtues are likewise pervasive. Although they are six when distinguished, they are but three when unified.

Third, regarding "three nines": "separately" means that the three aspects of cultivation and the three aspects of nature each constitute three dharmas, totaling nine; "combined" means that the two aspects of cultivation and the one aspect of nature constitute three dharmas.
Fourth, there are nine aspects of nature and eighteen aspects of cultivation, as described in the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* in the passage concerning the dream of the golden drum.
Now, it is said that "three-one-three-nine" represents the correct principle of separation and integration.

Cultivating the three natures involves three aspects; these belong to the cultivation arising from the totality of the nature itself, rather than being a matter of distinguishing between separation and integration.
Fifth, previously, when I received instruction from my teacher Qingbian, he once distinguished two meanings:
first, discussing the separation and union of cultivation and nature individually; second, discussing the separation and union of cultivation and nature in contrast to one another.
Furthermore, regarding each of these arguments, as stated in the *Jinbi*:
"Fundamentally there are three kinds; the three principles are originally pervasive. Since this resides within the nature, cultivation is entirely perfected within the nature."

The nature itself is originally free from the nine; by its own synthesis, it forms the three. When one realizes the nature, cultivation is perfected; the three aspects of cultivation are likewise pervasive. This is the arising of cultivation, whereby the entire nature becomes cultivation.
"Cultivation also involves nine [aspects], which together likewise constitute three.
This is discussed in terms of horizontal (transverse) analysis regarding two layers of separation and integration.
As for the vertical (correlative) analysis, it is as stated in the *Shiqian*:
"Separation" refers to the three types each of cultivation and nature; since the nature does not shift and cultivation remains ever distinct, there are nine dharmas.
"Combination" refers to two types of cultivation and one type of nature; this is discussed in terms of combination by contrasting the relative application of effort, addition, and subtraction.

"In the nature [of the Buddha], the conditions and the understanding are effortless; thus it is designated as 'one nature. When the dharmakāya and saṃbhogakāya of cultivated virtue receive permeation, they are termed 'two cultivations.
This concludes one section on the vertical discussion of separation and integration.

Sixth, as for "the ultimate meaning": the present school demonstrates this method of differentiation and integration (*li-he*) in order to reveal that the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inconceivable. Why is this?
Although it is discussed that the three are integrated into one, the one is not fixed as one; the one is inherently and eternally three.
Although it is shown that the one is divided into three, these three are not fixed as three; the three are themselves eternally one.
Therefore, Zhan’an said: "Transversely they are ever loftier;
vertically they are ever more expansive. When brought together, they always remain distinct; when branched out, they always remain united."
7. Regarding the classification of the teachings (*panjiao*), the *Golden Scalpel* (*Jinbi*) states:

"In discussing the two teachings concerning birth, it appears that both clarify the possession [of the Buddha-nature]. However, the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) does not explain the meaning of the 'possession of seeds' and so forth; thus, it cannot be described by this [criterion]."
Therefore, the distinct teaching (biejiao) differentiates the Buddha-nature and eliminates the nine perspectives of the square.

The person of the perfect teaching (yuanren), however, realizes that the three realms and the three paths of the nine realms are themselves the pervasive substance of the three virtues of the perfect *i* (the circular *i*).
Since the distinct teaching does not discuss the inherent possession of all seeds, it consequently speaks of the vertical and horizontal relationship between the cultivated and the innate.
"The Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) reveals that the essence is all-pervasive; therefore, it expounds the separation and union of cultivation and nature.
This demonstrates their commonality without confusion, and further clarifies that even in their separation, they are not divided.
8. Regarding the determination of stages: since the teaching is exclusively of the Perfect (yuan) nature, the stages must be distinguished to avoid confusion.
The first is restricted to the stage prior to abiding; the second applies to both the initial and final stages; and the third indicates the ultimate fruit.
First, regarding those who abide in the limited [view]:
The *Fumen* (Gate of Non-duality) states:
"Just as a mirror inherently possesses the three [aspects], when understanding arises based on principle, it is therefore called 'wisdom' (*jñāna*)."
"Wisdom and understanding guide practice, and practice and understanding accord with principle.
Since the three factors correspond in the first abode (*prathama-bhūmi*), the distinctions of granting and withholding, or separation and union, pertain only to the stages prior to this abode.
Second, regarding those that apply throughout both the initial and subsequent stages: [text follows].
The *Xianxing lu* states:
"Regarding the positions of the conditions (pratyaya) and the cause (hetu) within a single school, the distinctions of depth, shallowness, affirmation, and negation do not follow a single path.

For instance, according to the commentary on the 'Life Span' chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the stages prior to the [first] abiding are all collectively the condition-cause, while the first abiding itself is the truly manifest cause of realization."

Because one who hears the sutra according to the vehicle of the śrāvaka receives a prediction (vyākaraṇa) and immediately enters the first stage (prathama-bhūmi), this is distinguished in terms of the true and semblance [aspects] of the object-condition and the understanding-condition.

According to the commentary on the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter, up to the ultimate stage it is called the three types of wisdom (jñāna-traya); the four intermediate stages are all considered the three types of practice (caryā-traya).
This is because it follows the scriptural text to its ultimate conclusion in all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
This explains the distinct aspects of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the understanding-condition (*pariniṣpatti-pratyaya*).
As for the commentary on the "Dharma-preacher Chapter" (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*), the True Suchness prior to the Path is the Direct Cause (*hetu*).
The True Suchness within the process of the Path serves as the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) and is also termed the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*);
the True Suchness at the culmination of the Path is the perfect fruit (*pariniṣpanna-phala*).
The Record states:
This refers to cultivated virtue (bhāvanā-guṇa) in contrast to the direct cause (hetu).
Within the direct cause, the conditional cause (pratyaya) and the contributory cause (upaniṣad) together constitute the direct cause;
within cultivated virtue, the direct cause constitutes the conditional and contributory causes.
It is further stated:
"This divides the stages into two: taking the stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) as the 'pre-path' and the period after the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) as the 'middle path.
The stage prior to abiding (*vihāra*) is considered the 'condition,' while from the attainment of abiding onwards is considered the 'fulfillment.'"
"These three causes encompass the entirety of this teaching.
Third, regarding the demonstration of the ultimate fruit:
the *Nirvāṇa Xuán* explains "Great Parinirvāṇa" as follows:
The text states that even the Dharma-body is not [the ultimate]; how then can it be explained as the "Great" solely by means of the three bodies?
The text states that even liberation is not [the ultimate]; how then can it be explained as "Extinction" solely by means of the three liberations?
The text states: "If even Prajñā is not [the ultimate], how can one explain 'crossing over' (pāramitā) solely as the three types of wisdom?
The predecessors then asserted that since the Great Parinirvāṇa consists of three, and each of these is further divided into nine, they together constitute twenty-seven distinct dharmas.
Now, the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) by Zhāng'ān states:
"Though it is one, it is three; though it is three, it is one;
though it is both one and three, it is neither one nor three."
"Although it is neither three nor one, yet it is both three and one; it is inconceivable and encompasses all dharmas.

The Patriarch taught this to manifest the perfect fusion of the three virtues, which differs from any vertical, horizontal, or separate arrangement. Later descendants analyzed these into twenty-seven dharmas, which is far removed from the Way.
9. Resolving Doubts: Someone may ask, "If there are three dharmas within the nature, and two practices arise to manifest them, then it follows that there is only one dharma.
How can you say they are combined into one?"
Nanping Shi said:
"There is only one set of three virtues; they are spoken of as being either opened or closed.
If discussed from the perspective of delusion, then the three are combined into one."
If spoken of in terms of awakening, then cultivation and arising constitute two.
It is like the body and its arm: when bound, they merge into a single body; when released, they separate into three parts.
The former master explained:

"Though one engages in the two types of cultivation throughout the entire day while following conditions, what hindrance is there to the fact that within the nature there is no change throughout the entire day?
That which is called 'nature' is nowhere shifted; yet 'cultivation' remains ever distinct."
10. Regarding the corruption of the term "finger" (aṅguli), the "Chapter on Repentance" in the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* states: "There are two things seen and heard in dreams:
first, seeing a golden drum in a dream; second, hearing the sound of striking the drum in a dream."
There are three ways of seeing the drum:

first, by seeing the substance of the drum, one beholds the Dharma-body; second, by seeing the light of the drum, one beholds the Reward-body through the wisdom of light; third, by seeing the Buddha within the light, one beholds the Response-body, for that Buddha is the Response-body itself.
Second, the dream of beating a drum.
This consists of three parts:

first, seeing the drum being beaten; second, the emergence of a great sound; third, the meaning conveyed by the sound, which distinguishes that the drum is the *dharmakāya*, the union of the drumstick and the drum is the *saṃbhogakāya*, and the striking that produces the sound is the *nirmāṇakāya*.
The ancients held that seeing a golden drum in a dream represents the nine dharmas within the nature—three for each of the three bodies.
Seeing the drum being struck represents the nine dharmas within cultivation. Thus, they spoke of twenty-seven dharmas, comprising three sets of nine.
The New Commentary refutes this, saying:
"In the preceding text, the three [aspects] of the drum represent the three aspects of the Dharma-body, which are the three aspects of the objective realm.
The three [aspects] of the drum's light represent the three aspects of wisdom."
The three instances of seeing the Buddha correspond to the three [applications].
The current text merely clarifies the person who strikes; it speaks of using wisdom to strike the drum—how could it ever discuss the twenty-seven dharmas of cultivation and nature?
Furthermore, as the *Records of the Four Clarities* states:
"The upper drum symbolizes the three luminaries and the three Buddhas; the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* constitute one three.

Now, in accordance with what is observed by the wisdom of those at the stage of faith, the three are merged into one and are simply termed the Dharma-body; this is the clear mirror of the mutual fusion and identity of cultivation and nature."
Those who study this school should understand that the three dots of the character *i* represent the world, and the three eyes of the Lord of Heaven.
They distinguish themselves from the vertical and horizontal arrangements of other teachings, establishing the union and separation of the Perfect School.
This reveals the identity between cultivation and nature, and unifies sentient beings and Buddhas as sharing a single source.
It transcends the gateway of thought and deliberation; it is a dharma beyond calculation or measure.
Thus, when Vimalakīrti’s words ceased at Vaiśālī and Śākyamuni’s speech was exhausted at Magadha, it was named the "Inconceivable Dharma."

56. Chapter on Afflictions, Delusions, and Karma. Chapter Fifty-Six: Afflictions, Bodhi, and their Essential Unity. The essence of afflictions and bodhi is fundamentally one; it is only through the views of nirvana and birth-and-death that they appear as two.
If one knows the nature of reality as it is and understands the illusory character of phenomena, one employs the wisdom of compassion to remedy greed, hatred, and delusion.
Thus, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "Distant from all afflictions, pure and stainless like the ultimate truth, the mind then becomes a great radiance; this is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī."
[Ālaya]: The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because it relies upon the ālayavijñāna, there is said to be ignorance (*avidyā*), which arises through non-awakening as:

(1) the characteristic of the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), which is able to see; (2) the characteristic of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), which is able to manifest; and (3) the characteristic of the manifesting consciousness (*darśanavijñāna*), which is able to grasp objects and give rise to a continuous stream of thought; therefore, it is called 'mind' (*manas*)."
This clarifies that with ignorance (*avidyā*) as a condition, the three subtle states arise, which are termed the delusion of ignorance;

with objective realms as a condition, the six coarse states arise: first, the characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*); second, the characteristic of continuity (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*); third, the characteristic of grasping (*upādāna-lakṣaṇa*); fourth, the characteristic of calculating names (*nāma-saṃkhyā-vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*); fifth, the characteristic of initiating karma (*karma-pravartana-lakṣaṇa*); and sixth, the characteristic of suffering bound by karma (*karma-bandhana-duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*). These are termed the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kāma-āsrava*).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the fundamental affliction; it obstructs the principle of the Middle Way, and one should practice the Middle Way contemplation (*madhyamaka-vipaśyanā*) to destroy this specific delusion.

Views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are the derivative afflictions; they obstruct the principle of the True Truth (*satya*), and one should practice the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) to destroy these pervasive delusions.
When the delusions of the general and specific categories have vanished, the principles of Reality and the Middle Way manifest of themselves.
[Sakāya]: The commentary notes that the full form is *sakāyadṛṣṭi*.
This is called the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The *Commentary on the Hundred Dharmas* states:
"It refers to the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self within the five aggregates; its function is to serve as the basis for all types of views."
*Dṛṣṭi* (view) is translated here as "seeing. There are five types of views: first, *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (the view of a self-identity), which clings to the notion of a self and what belongs to a self;

second, *antagrāhadṛṣṭi* (the view of extremes), which follows the former to calculate either annihilationism or eternalism; third, *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (the clinging to views), which clings to that which is inferior and regards it as superior; fourth, *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (the clinging to precepts and observances), which regards what is not a cause as a cause; and fifth, *mithyādṛṣṭi* (wrong view), which denies the existence of cause and effect and the dharmas thereof.
Possessing these five types is called "delusion through views" (dṛṣṭi-kleśa).
The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:
"Seeing refers to seeing the principle; seeing reality is not delusion."

"At the time one perceives the principle, one is able to sever these delusions; because they are named according to their cessation through understanding, they are called 'delusions of view' (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

Furthermore, the delusions of view are not only named according to their cessation through understanding, but they also receive their name based on their own essential nature, being designated as 'provisional' (*prajñapti*)."
The "provisional" (prajñapti) refers to that which is false and inverted; it is merely designated as "provisional.
One should know that there are three types of afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*):
first, innate views (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*); second, views derived from inference (*tarka-dṛṣṭi*); and third, views acquired through realization (*abhinirhāra-dṛṣṭi*).
First, regarding innate views (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*), the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:

"Why must the five dull afflictions necessarily be greed and anger? Consider wriggling insects: though they truly do not engage in reasoning, they raise their antennae, spread their fins, glare with angry eyes, and act with self-importance."
As for the ordinary beings below, when have they ever been free from clinging views?
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, they constantly give rise to the notion of "self.
Thus we know that the five dull afflictions are not without their corresponding sharp ones.
The *Jì* (Commentary) says:

"Among those who are dull-witted, there are those who possess sharp faculties; for instance, even insects, beasts, and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) can give rise to the notion of 'I. This 'I' is itself a sharp faculty, yet though it is sharp, it remains subordinate to their dullness."
It further states:
"Although those of inferior capacity may give rise to [the aspiration for] benefit, this benefit belongs to the dull faculty; it arises from behind the dull underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Second, the inference of views, as stated in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*:

"Now, if we divide them according to their stages so that they do not overlap: prior to the arising of dhyāna, although one may possess worldly wisdom, logical reasoning, and eloquence, one's views and perceptions remain weak; thus, all ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are categorized as dull."
The *Jì* (Commentary) states:

"Before one has attained dhyāna, even if latent predispositions arise, all afflictions (*kleśa*) as well as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) arising from the aggregates (*skandha*) due to [wrong] views still belong to the dull fetters (*mṛdu-kleśa*).
These are abandoned by the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), are shared by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), lie dormant within the body, and obstruct true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*)."
"If one perceives the principle of the Truths (*satya*), these delusions are eliminated of their own accord.
Therefore, this delusion is designated as 'seeing' (*darśana*); thus, it differs from that which arises subsequent to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Third, "arousing and attaining seeing," the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:

"From concentration arising from causes, views are produced; when the mind of views is intense and flourishing, the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) receive their names based on their strength, and all belong to the category of 'sharp' [afflictions].
The *Commentary* states:

"If various non-Buddhists, because they have not yet seen the Truths, attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), they may sever the dull underlying tendencies, yet they have never severed even a hair’s breadth of the delusions of view."

Because the afflictions of views (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) are manifest [at this stage], they differ from those views that have not yet arisen during the practice of dhyāna, as well as those that remain latent; therefore, the views among the eighty-eight proclivities (anuśaya) are not used as the standard example here.
Therefore, the meaning of the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) is subsumed within the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*).

To speak briefly, there are three fetters (*saṃyojana*); to explain extensively, there are the eighty-eight proclivities. Now, the verse is stated as follows: "The ten proclivities pertain to the Truth of Suffering; seven each to Origination and Cessation;

the three—view of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—are absent [from the higher realms]. On the Path Truth, only the two—view of self-identity and view of extremes—are removed. Above [the Desire Realm], anger is not present; thus they total eighty-eight."

Briefly stated, the three fetters are: first, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); second, attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); and third, the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā*).
When greed and anger are added to these, they are called the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).
As the *Myōraku* states:
Regarding the "lower fetters": although craving extends upward, it is not exclusively of the upper realm.
Hatred is exclusively lower and does not extend upward at all; the remaining three encompass all delusions of view.
Now the question is asked:
"Since [the path of] vision (darśana-mārga) encompasses all five faculties of the利 (sharp/wholesome), why does the *Abhidharmakośa* speak only of three fetters (saṃyojana)? Answer:
As the verse of the treatise says:
"Because it subsumes the gates of the faculties.
Regarding the "gates of the faculties," the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is itself the gate of suffering.
The clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) pertains to the two gates of suffering and the path;
doubt (*vicikitsā*) pervades all four gates, namely the Four Noble Truths.

Regarding what is called the "inclusion of the faculties" (*indriya-saṃgraha*): the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arise based on the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) arises based on the clinging to precepts and observances; and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) arise based on doubt. Therefore, these three fetters (*saṃyojana*) subsume the five views.
Question:

“Since the delusions of view (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) already span the four truths across the three realms, how can it be said that the remaining three [categories of affliction] universally encompass all delusions of view?
Although they extend upward, do they not also pull down those below?”
The answer is:
“Although the truths that are the objects of delusion pervade all three realms, the afflictions capable of pulling one back reside specifically in the desire realm.

Therefore it is said that even if one has severed craving and so forth up to the sphere of nothingness, one returns to the desire realm due to the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and other such afflictions.”
Question:
As stated in the *Miaoxuan*:
"Having severed the delusions of the Truths (satyadarśana-heya), one further eliminates the four types of [wholesome] volition."
"I do not yet understand which dharma constitutes volition.
He replied:
"This refers to the volitions of the four destinies, which constitute the four types of volition."

Based on the *Myōgen* (The Profound Meaning), because it clarifies causes and benefits, observing the precepts while still at the stage of an ordinary person subdues the karma of the four miserable realms;
practicing contemplation upon attaining the first fruit of sainthood severs the volitional impulses leading to those four realms.
"Because the two types of volition (saṃskāra) associated with innate [delusion] follow the fall of views, they are said to be 'removed concurrently.
One should know that there are three kinds of afflictions of volition:
first, innate volition."

Arising together with the physical form, it is like a male or female entering a womb; to falsely harbor thoughts of love or hatred toward one's parents is a perverse thought, which ultimately returns to the delusion of views.
Second, regarding [the distinction between] views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*).
The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:
"How could the five sharp faculties be limited to delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) alone? Have they ever been devoid of anger and desire?"
The *Record* says:
"Among those of sharp faculties, there are those of dull faculties, such as the various non-Buddhists who give rise to anger based on their various views.
Question:
The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* says:
"If there is dullness within sharpness, then upon seeing the truths, only the sharp [afflictions] are severed.
Does the dullness still remain?
Answer: According to the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (or *Zhi guan*), the Abhidharma states that those who are dull among the sharp are called "latent tendencies on the back" (*pṛṣṭhata-anuśaya*).
When the truths are realized (*satyadarśana-prahāṇa*), the primary sharpness is eliminated, and the latent tendencies on the back are likewise eliminated.
3. Afflictions bound to the realms (*dhātu-saṃyojana-cetanā*).
These are the nine grades of afflictions of volition within the three realms.
They are termed "dull fetters" (*mṛdu-kleśa*), also called "obstructions of phenomena" (*vastu-āvaraṇa*), and are designated as the "innate three poisons. As Du Mu once said: [text follows].
Now, among the seven emotions, love and anger are those with which one is naturally endowed at birth. These two are the root of human nature and the source of evil.
When an infant sees its mother’s breast, it instinctively grasps for it; if it does not obtain what it seeks, it cries. Thus, love and anger are born together with the child.
Question: "The five higher fetters are:

first, restlessness and haughtiness, which are the outflows of greed; second, pride; third, ignorance; fourth, attachment to the realm of form; and fifth, attachment to the formless realm. Because greed is predominant, these two realms are explained separately."
"Why is there no doubt in the higher realms? Answer:
"Doubt falls away following views; therefore, this delusion does not exist there."
The *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā* correlates the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) with the four [unwholesome] roots; it assigns greed, anger, sleep, and doubt to delusion (*moha*).
The *Jì* states: "One sleeps because of delusion; one doubts because of delusion."
"Restlessness and scattering" refers to my grasping; the *Ji* (Record) states:
"Because the mind of grasping gives rise universally to the three poisons, it is called restlessness and scattering."
The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:
"There are three kinds of restlessness (*auddhatya*):
first, physical restlessness, which is a fondness for wandering about, various frivolous amusements, and an inability to remain seated even for a moment."

Second is verbal restlessness (*vāg-auddhatya*): being fond of chanting and recitation, competing over right and wrong, engaging in unprofitable frivolous talk (*prapañca*), worldly speech, and the like.

Third is mental restlessness (*citta-auddhatya*): the mind being lax and negligent, allowing the faculties to wander toward objects of perception, contemplating literature and arts, worldly skills and talents, various evil thoughts and reflections (*vitarka-vicāra*), and so forth; this is called mental restlessness.
Each of these four produces twenty-one thousand [afflictions].

The new *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra states: "Those with a predominance of greed have twenty-one thousand; those with a predominance of anger have twenty-one thousand; those with a predominance of delusion have twenty-one thousand; and those with equal proportions of all three have twenty-one thousand. One should fully understand that all of these are entirely false and illusory."
Chuiyu explains that the ten entanglements (*daśa-paryavasthāna*) are afflictions of thought (*vicikitsā-kleśa*):
"Anger and resentment are called *pratigha* (hatred);
concealing one's own transgressions is called *mrakṣa* (concealment)."
The state in which consciousness is clouded is called sleep;
the state in which the five sensory faculties are darkened is called slumber;
and frolicking about is called play.
The restlessness of the three types of action is called *auddhatya* (restlessness);
to commit an offense in private without feeling shame for oneself is called *āhrīkya* (lack of self-respect);
to commit an offense in public without feeling shame before others is called *anapatrāpya* (lack of decorum).
"Not being able to give away wealth or the Dharma with wisdom is called stinginess (*mātsarya*);
for another's prosperity to cause heat and affliction in one's mind is called envy (*īrṣyā*).
The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* says:
"The eight envelopments (paryavasthāna) are shamelessness (āhrīkya), lack of dread (anapatrāpya), envy (īrṣyā), parsimony (mātsarya), along with regret (kaukṛtya), torpor (middha);
as well as restlessness (auddhatya) and lethargy (styāna). Alternatively, there are ten [envelopments] when anger (krodha) and concealment (mrakṣa) are added.
The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* clarifies the ten habitual tendencies (daśa-vāsanā):
"1. Regarding the first, the *Jiexu* (Commentary on the Sections) states: "

1. Sexual habituation refers to the karma produced by it, which is fully endowed with greed and delusion; 2. Greed is included among the categories of the root of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); 3. Pride consists of relying on oneself to despise others, having the nature of loftiness; 4. Anger is the state of being heated and distressed within the heart, having the nature of lack of peace and stability; 5. Deceit refers to flattery and crookedness, which involves deceiving others and falsely assuming an artificial demeanor, having the nature of flattery and crookedness, and taking wrong livelihood as its function; 6. Guile refers to hypocrisy, harboring ulterior motives and frequently manifesting what is unreal, falsely appearing to possess virtue, having the nature of craftiness and deception, and taking wrong livelihood as its function; 7. Enmity is resentment, which, preceded by anger, involves harboring malice without relinquishing it, having the nature of forming a grudge, being unable to endure, and constantly being distressed; 8. Views refer to the five types of views.
The *Fuxing* states:
"The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 23, says: 'It refers to being separated from five matters, which are the five views.
Based on these five views, the sixty-two [views] arise.'"
Zhang’an said: “This has two meanings.
First, there are fifty-six types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of self): regarding the five aggregates (*skandha*) of the desire realm, each is reckoned as four propositions, totaling twenty;
the same applies to the form realm. In the formless realm, excluding form, there are sixteen.”
Thus, it is known that there are fifty-six views in the three realms.

There are six extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), two for each of the three realms—namely, the views of nihilism and eternalism—which, when added to the preceding, constitute the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭidṛṣṭi*).

Second, regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the three periods of time, each is reckoned as either annihilated or eternal, taking the two views of existence and non-existence as their root.
This is based on the text of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 68.
That is to say, there are four propositions regarding form as "gone" and so forth; the same applies to the other four aggregates.
Together these constitute twenty propositions, which constitute the reckoning of the past.

Furthermore, there are four propositions regarding form as "permanent" and so forth; the same applies to the other four aggregates. Together these constitute twenty propositions, which constitute the reckoning of the present.

Furthermore, calculating the four propositions such as "form has limits" and so forth, and likewise for the other four aggregates, results in twenty propositions; this constitutes the calculation regarding the future.
Including the three time periods, there are sixty, plus the two views of existence and non-existence.

9. Deceit (*māyā*) refers to the oppression of the virtuous; it is subsumed under harm and is also a category of hatred (*dveṣa*). 10. Slander (*śāṭhya*) refers to the habit of disputing gain and loss; with resentment as its precursor, it is a single dharma of affliction (*upāyāsa*), for its nature is associated with that [resentment].
*Niyan-ti* (尼延底) means "deep entry" (*praveśa*) and is a synonym for craving (*rāga*).
Attachment to pleasure is termed craving.
There are two types of persons who crave:
First, there is the powerful; second, there is the powerless.
Regarding the objects of craving, the *Chanmen* (The Gate of Dhyāna) clarifies three types:
first, external desire, wherein a man takes a woman as his object and a woman takes a man as her object.
2. Internal and external lust: externally taking the physical forms of men and women as objects, and internally taking one's own physical appearance as an object.
3. Lust pervading all places: sentient beings are attached everywhere.
The *Abhidharmakośa* clarifies four types:
first, color-form (*varṇa-rūpa*), which refers to blue, yellow, red, and white;
second, shape-form (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), which refers to long, short, square, round, and so forth.
Third, exquisite touch; fourth, service and offerings.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies six types:
first, attachment to color—whether red, white, yellow, or black.
Second, some become attached to physical appearance—delicate skin, slender fingers, long eyes, and high eyebrows.

Third, some become attached to deportment and movement—sitting, rising, walking, and standing; bowing, looking up, and looking down; raising the eyebrows, blinking the eyes, and engaging in close physical contact such as massage.
Fourth, they may become attached to speech—soft voices and elegant words that accord with one's own mind and fulfill one's intentions.
Fifth, they may become attached to smoothness—the soft skin and supple flesh that feels cool to the body in the heat and warm to the limbs in the cold.
Sixth, one may be attached to the mark of a person, whether male or female.
*Kaṭasi* is here translated as a specific name for craving.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The swirling currents of the river of craving submerge sentient beings; blinded by ignorance, they cannot escape.
Regarding greed (*rāga*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), Guifeng’s *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra Commentary* explains them through four permutations:

first, greed that is not craving, such as when a person craves busyness, yet this is not a matter of loving busyness; second, craving that is not greed, such as when a person loves to watch people fighting or killing one another—who would ever crave or seek such things?; third, both greed and craving, namely fame, profit, wealth, and sensual beauty; and fourth, neither greed nor craving, namely objects that are contrary to one's desires.
The *Guǎnzǐ* says:
"Where profit lies, there is no mountain of a thousand *zhèn* that it will not ascend, and no deep abyss below which it will not enter."
Merchants engage in trade, doubling their pace and traveling by day and night; for them, a thousand li is not far when profit lies ahead.
Fishermen enter the sea where the waters are a hundred fathoms deep and the surging waves crash forward; they do not emerge for days and nights because profit lies in the water.
The Fisherman said:
"A person has eight defects:
to occupy oneself with affairs that are not one's own is called 'muddled,' which is a form of impropriety."
To insist on knowing matters that do not concern oneself is called audacity and immodesty.
To advance [counsel] when it is disregarded is called sycophancy; to offer loyal words which people do not heed or accept is called flattery.
To guide speech with a view toward one's own desires is called *chǎn* (flattery); it means to guide one's words so as to anticipate and comply with the intentions and temperaments of others.
To speak without distinguishing between right and wrong is called *yútí* (sycophancy); it means to follow others with fawning compliance, making no selection between what is right and what is wrong.
To delight in speaking of others' evils is called calumny; to hear of others' faults and take pleasure in proclaiming them is likewise so.
To sever friendships and alienate kin is called treachery; when people have ties of affection or old acquaintances, one who seeks immediately to divide and alienate them is an accomplice to harm.

They praise the deceitful and sell themselves as virtuous people; they claim that those close to them are to be praised even if they are wicked, while those distant from them are to be disparaged even if they are good.

To fail to distinguish between good and evil, to tolerate both equally for the sake of personal comfort, and to perversely extract whatever one desires—this is called "perilousness" (險), which is wickedness.
It is to admit both extremes of good and evil without discrimination.
"With a pleasant countenance and a cheerful expression, one stealthily extracts what the other desires and flatters them accordingly;
such a person is treacherous and perverse. These eight defects disturb others externally and injure oneself internally.
The gentleman does not take him as a friend, and the enlightened ruler does not employ him as a minister.
In the "Fisherman" chapter:
"There are four kinds of calamities in service:..."
To covet great affairs, to alter and change established norms, and to seek fame and merit—this is called *dào* (presumptuousness). The commentary states:

To bide one's time while watching for security or peril, to manage great undertakings, and to establish fame and merit at the moment of transformation and change—these are called the actions of a presumptuous and overreaching person.
To monopolize knowledge and usurp affairs, encroaching upon others for one's own use, is called greed. The commentary states:
"To be exclusive and self-possessive, using oneself to overstep others, is called greed."
To see one's faults yet not change them, and upon hearing admonition to become even more obstinate—this is called "obduracy. The commentary states:
"One who does not reform their transgressions and, upon hearing counsel, increases their perversity is called an obdurate and violent person."
If others are the same as oneself, one may accept them; if they are not the same as oneself, then regardless of whether they are good or bad, one treats them with disdain. The commentary states:
"When things are the same as oneself, even if they are evil, one regards them as good;
when things differ from oneself, even if they are good, one regards them as evil—this is called a person of arrogance and self-aggrandizement."
“*Tivisa*”: this is translated as “anger” (*dveṣa*).
“Anger” refers to resentment and hatred.
The *Chanmen* (Dhyāna Gate) clarifies three types of anger: [text continues]
First, irrational anger: one gives rise to anger spontaneously even though the other person has not come to cause provocation.
Second, rational anger: one gives rise to anger only when an external person comes to cause provocation.
It is also like the Pure Land, where there exist the three primary poisons.

Third is the poison of contention and anger: being attached to one's own doctrine as being right and declaring the doctrines of others to be wrong; due to this lack of compliance, the perception of affliction arises.
[Mu-he]: This is translated as "delusion" (moha).
The *Chanmen* (Gate of Meditation) clarifies three types of delusion:
first, calculating [the extremes of] annihilationism and eternalism—asking whether past phenomena have ceased to exist, or whether present phenomena do not cease to exist.
Investigating the three periods of time: if they cease, they are annihilated; if they do not cease, they are eternal.
Second, calculating existence and non-existence: do the self, the aggregates, and so forth exist, or do they not?
Thus it continues up to "neither existent nor non-existent.
Third, regarding the calculation of the nature of the world, they form this thought:
"Because there are subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), there are therefore real dharmas."
Because there are real dharmas, there are the four great elements;
because there are the four great elements, there are provisional names.
It is due to such conceptualization that sentient beings in the world practice the path of error.
In the *Āgama*, the *Sūtra on Right Practice*, it is said: "The Buddha sat in meditation and reflected:
'It is because of delusion that there is birth and death.
What is this delusion?'"
Originally arising from ignorance, one is born as a human being yet remains deluded.
The mind finds no understanding and achieves no self-awakening; one does not know where one shall go when death occurs.
Seeing the Buddha, one does not inquire; seeing the scriptures, one does not read; seeing śramaṇas, one does not serve them.

To lack faith in the Way and its virtue, to see one's parents without reverence, to fail to contemplate the suffering of the world, and to be ignorant of the severe punishments in the hells—this is called delusion; therefore, there is birth and death.
Birth and death do not last longer than the interval between a single inhalation and exhalation; human life is no more enduring than something as fragile as a piece of raw meat.
Yet these—greed, anger, and delusion—are called the three poisons.
The *Sūtra on the Intermediate State* (*Zhongyin jing*) states:
"Among the three poisons, the most grave is the disease of delusion (*moha*), which is their source.
Furthermore, these three poisons must be divided into two types:
The first is the delusion of the three poisons.
The *Bie xing ji* states:
"That which arises spontaneously is called affliction (*kleśa*)."
The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:
"The dharmas of dullness and affliction disturb and disorder the mind; they create affliction for the mind and cause the mind to experience distress.
Second, the karma of the three poisons. The *Bie xing ji* states:
"When a decision suddenly arises and is able to move the body and speech, it is called the karma of the three poisons.
The *Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra* states:
"Greed leads to old age; hatred leads to illness; delusion leads to death; by extension, the equal combination [of these] leads to birth."
Furthermore, one must know that karma is of many kinds.
As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
"Black karma refers to unwholesome karma."
The places of suffering and affliction, such as the hells of retribution, are called "black" because the sentient beings therein are overwhelmed by extreme great pain and distress.
The places where one receives the retribution of wholesome fruits—namely, the various heavens—are called "white karma" because they experience pleasure that is spontaneous, sovereign, and clear.

This karma belongs to the heavens of the three realms and is the locus for experiencing the retributions of both wholesome and unwholesome deeds—namely, the eight classes of beings such as humans and asuras. Because one experiences both pleasure and suffering in these places, it is called "white-black" karma.
Question:
"Untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) ought to be white; why then do you say it is neither white nor black? Answer:
"Although untainted dharmas are pure and stainless, because they are empty, signless, and wishless, they are without discrimination; thus, one cannot say they are white.
Black and white are relative phenomena; since there is no relativity herein, one cannot say they are white."

Furthermore, untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) can extinguish all forms of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); because there is conceptual differentiation within contemplation, there is "black" and "white," but since there is no contemplation herein, there is no "white," and so forth.
However, the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Bequeathed Teaching) states:
"I am like a skilled physician who, knowing the disease, prescribes the medicine.
The *Myōgen* (Miaoxuan) states:
"One who acts as a Great King of Physicians must understand the various pulses and diseases, recognize the various medicines, master the various treatments, and achieve various cures.
The *Renyō-kyō* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states:
"The Buddha knows that sentient beings have three kinds of illnesses:"
"First is the disease of greed, second is the disease of anger, and third is the disease of delusion.
Having recognized these diseases, one should apply the medicine.
Thus, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* says:
"To remedy the three unwholesome roots of greed, hatred, and delusion, one gives rise to the three wholesome roots of generosity, loving-kindness, and wisdom.
To remedy greed, one is taught to practice giving; thus the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* states:
"One relinquishes all that is most cherished, including one's limbs, joints, hands, and feet."
To remedy anger, one is taught to practice loving-kindness and compassion; thus the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"Always gentle and able to endure, showing compassion toward all.
To remedy delusion, one is taught to cultivate wisdom; thus the *Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching* says:
"True wisdom is a sturdy ship for crossing the ocean of old age, sickness, and death; it is also a great bright lamp in the darkness of ignorance.
Although this medicine exists, whether one takes it or not is not the fault of the physician.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* says:
"For example, one who possesses excellent remedies cannot cure their own illness;
likewise, it is the same for those who do not practice the Dharma despite having heard much."
*Ājīvika*: This is translated as "wrong livelihood," meaning one sustains the life-root through false teachings.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"As it is said in the Sūtras, Śāriputra entered the city to beg for food; having obtained it, he sat against a wall to eat."
At that time, a brahmin girl named Viśākhā saw him and asked,
"Śramaṇa, will you eat? He replied:
"Eat. Viśuddhanetra asked,
"Do you eat with food placed directly into the mouth?"
Do you eat by looking upward?
Do you eat by facing forward?
Or do you eat by facing the four intermediate directions?
They both replied,
"No. Viśuddhanetra said:
“There are four kinds of lawful food.
I ask you about them; you say ‘no,’ which I do not understand.
You should explain.”
Śāriputra said:
"There are renunciants who compound medicines, sow grain, and plant trees; they sustain their lives through impure means, which is called 'eating from below.

There are renunciants who observe the stars and constellations, the sun and moon, wind and rain, thunder, lightning, and peals of thunder; they sustain their lives through impure means, which is called 'eating from above.'"

There are those who have left the household life who flatter and curry favor with those of power and influence, acting as messengers to all quarters; they employ clever speech to seek much for themselves, sustaining their lives through impure means—this is called "eating from every direction."
"There are those who have left the household life who study various incantations and arts, divining good and ill fortune to sustain their lives; this is called 'feeding on the four directions.
Sister!
I do not fall into these four kinds of impure food; I sustain my life through the pure alms-seeking of a mendicant."
At that time, Viśuddhanetra, hearing the teaching on the food of pure Dharma, rejoiced with faith and understanding.
Śāriputra then preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the Eightfold Noble Path as follows:
"The five kinds of wrong livelihood are abandoned by means of untainted wisdom; this is right livelihood."
Question:
"What are the five kinds of wrong livelihood? Answer:
"First, for the sake of gain and offerings, they falsely manifest extraordinary feats;
second, for the sake of gain and offerings, they speak of their own merits;
third, for the sake of gain and offerings, they practice divination of auspicious and inauspicious signs."
Fourth, for the sake of gain and offerings, they raise their voices and manifest an air of authority to cause others to feel fear and reverence;
fifth, for the sake of gain and offerings, they proclaim the offerings they have received in order to stir the hearts of people.
"Because one sustains life through improper causes and conditions, this is called wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
[Ārāga]: This is translated here as "desire"; its meaning is that which is longed for or sought after.
That which is desired by the five sensory faculties is termed the "five desires" (*pañcakāmaguṇa*).
The *Mahā-śāstra* states:
"Alas for sentient beings!
They are constantly tormented by the five desires, yet they seek them without ceasing."
These five desires, once obtained, only intensify further, like roasting scabies with fire.
The five desires are of no benefit, like a dog gnawing on a bone.
The five desires increase contention, like crows competing for meat.
The five desires burn people like holding a torch against the wind;
the five desires harm people like treading upon a venomous snake;
the five desires lack reality, like what is obtained in a dream.
The five desires are not enduring; they are but borrowed for a fleeting moment.
Worldly people, deluded by ignorance, are greedily attached to these five desires, failing to abandon them until death, thereby undergoing immeasurable suffering in future lives.
It is like a foolish person who, greedy for fine fruit, climbs a tree to eat it and refuses to descend in a timely manner.
When others cut down the tree, he falls as it topples over; his body and head are shattered, and he dies in agony.
However, these five desires pertain to both the internal and external realms.
As the *Mahāśāstra* states:
"The followers of the Two Vehicles sever only the five desires of the internal realm; therefore, they cannot be moved by the five desires of the mundane world."
"Because residual delusions have not yet been eliminated, one remains defiled by the exquisite forms and sounds beyond the realms.
Thus Kāśyapa said:
"The five desires of the three realms have already been severed by me; they cannot move my mind."
"These are the pure and exquisite five desires of a bodhisattva; I cannot find peace in these matters.
This was Kāśyapa being moved by sounds from outside his boundary.
When the heavenly maidens scattered flowers and Śāriputra removed them, this was a movement of forms external to his own realm.
Furthermore, to discriminate between birth-and-death and nirvana as being different is itself a separate view; this is to be deluded by the objects of the dharma-dust.
【Śatha】 This translates as "flattery" or "deviousness.
Because one deceives and misleads others, one feigns unusual conduct to pander crookedly to the people of the time.
Section 57: Mind, Consciousness, and Mental Factors. Section Fifty-Seven on Mind, Consciousness, and Mental Factors. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"The accumulation of various false karmas is called the mind (*citta*); the *manas* deliberates, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) discriminates, and the five sensory consciousnesses, such as that of the eye, perceive objects differently.
Foolish ordinary beings are unable to awaken to this; fearing old age, sickness, and death, they seek to enter nirvana."
"Failing to recognize both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, they give rise to false discrimination regarding all objects.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"Briefly stated, there are three kinds of consciousness; in detail, there are eight aspects."
What are these three?
They are the True Consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*). The *Zongjing* states:
"It is not defiled by impure dharmas; how much less is it treated as something to be remedied by pure dharmas."
"It is not that which is bound by birth and death, nor can it be stilled by nirvana.
Thus it is called the Lord of Consciousness, and is therefore named the King of the Mind.
[This refers to] the manifesting consciousness and the discriminating consciousness of phenomena.
"Mahāmati!
Just as a bright mirror holds all forms and images, so too is the locus where the manifesting consciousness appears. The *Ghanavyūha Sūtra* says:
'For example, like a supreme jewel that is despised by commoners, yet when used to adorn a ceremonial crown, it is worn upon the head of a king.'"
Thus, the ālayavijñāna is the pure Buddha-nature; though it is perpetually defiled during the stage of an ordinary being, it is eternally maintained at the stage of Buddhahood.
It is like a fine jade submerged in water, enveloped and concealed by a layer of moss.
The ālayavijñāna dwells within birth and death, its latent tendencies (vāsanā) so entangled that it does not manifest.
Within this ālayavijñāna, the two modes of grasping arise;
like a snake with two heads, they move together according to their inclination.
The ālayavijñāna is likewise; it coexists with all forms and characteristics.
All the worlds grasp it and take it to be form.
Those of deluded discernment are confused, reckoning it as "self" and "what belongs to self."
Whether existent or non-existent, Īśvara creates the world;
though the ālayavijñāna manifests transformations, its essential nature is eternally profound.
To those who lack wisdom, it remains entirely beyond their comprehension.

"Mahāmati! The manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) and the discriminating consciousness of objects (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*)—these two possess the characteristics of being perishable and imperishable. When the five consciousnesses perceive objects, they immediately cease; this is their perishability."

Infused into the eight consciousnesses as seeds, these constitute the indestructible, reciprocal causes: the seven consciousnesses grasp the eighth consciousness as a self, and the eighth consciousness induces the five consciousnesses to apprehend objects.
Mahāmati!
Regarding "inconceivable perfuming," Xianshou said:
"It means that ignorance is able to perfume True Suchness; because it perfumes that which cannot be perfumed, it is called 'inconceivable perfuming.'"
"Furthermore, perfuming is non-perfuming; this perfuming that is non-perfuming is called inconceivable perfuming.

Moreover, "inconceivable transformation" refers to the Tathāgatagarbha mind being perfumed by ignorance; although it is inherently unchangeable, it undergoes transformation, and is therefore termed inconceivable transformation.
Furthermore, transformation is itself non-transformation; this transformation of non-transformation is called "inconceivable transformation.

In the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, that which is difficult to comprehend—being defiled yet undefiled, and undefiled yet defiled—is precisely this inconceivability. This refers to the subtle activity of the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) arising from its cause. Within it, there are also the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*); however, because the gross is cited to reveal the subtle, it is designated solely as the manifesting consciousness, which is the mind of non-correspondence (*asamprayukta-citta*).

Mahāmati! The grasping of various objects is precisely the realm manifested by the *darśana-vijñāna* (perceiving consciousness), which in turn stirs that ocean of mind, giving rise to the waves of the various *vastu-vijñānas* (object-consciousnesses). Furthermore, beginningless false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) perfumes [the mind]; within that harmonious ocean of mind, the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of deluded thought have been perfuming it uninterruptedly since time immemorial, never having been separated from thought. Therefore, these objects and thoughts perfume and stir the ocean of mind, causing the various forms of consciousness to arise.

Because false thoughts and sensory objects are both manifest, the modes of activity of the discriminating consciousness of phenomena (*vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna*) become clearly manifest, forming the associated mind; this is the cause of the discriminating consciousness of phenomena.
It further states:
"For example, it is like the vast ocean waves, which arise from a fierce wind; the great billows surge through the depths of the abyss without ceasing for a moment.
The ocean of the *ālayavijñāna* is eternally abiding. As the *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* says:

"The World-Honored One is preaching the Dharma on Mount Laṅkā in the midst of the Southern Ocean. This mountain is steep and lofty, looking down upon the great sea, with no gates or entrances on its sides.
Only those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are capable of ascending and dwelling there."
This then manifests the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground; only those who realize through a mindless state can ascend.

Looking down upon the great ocean symbolizes that the ocean of the mind is inherently pure, yet it is stirred by the winds of external objects, causing the waves of consciousness to fluctuate. To clarify this, one must realize that when the objects of perception are empty, the mind is also empty, and the objects themselves naturally become still.
When both mind and objects are tranquil, there is nothing that is not illuminated.
It is like a great ocean without wind, where the sun, moon, and constellations shine with brilliant clarity.

The intent of this sutra is to directly teach those whose faculties are matured through the sudden approach, asserting that the seed-consciousness and karmic consciousness are the Tathāgatagarbha; it differs from the followers of the Two Vehicles who extinguish consciousness to seek quiescence, and it also surpasses the Bodhisattvas of the Prajñā school who cultivate emptiness. Therefore, it directly clarifies that the essential nature of consciousness is entirely true, and immediately shows that the substance of consciousness itself constitutes the function of wisdom—just as when the ocean is windless, the reflections of the environment naturally appear with clarity.

Unlike that *Saṃdhinirmocana*, which establishes nine distinct consciousnesses to guide those of initial capacity, gradually causing them to retain afflictions in order to grow their great bodhi, [this system] does not cause the mind to plant its seeds in emptiness, nor does it allow the mind to become like a rotten seed.
