Based on the perception (*darśana-bhāga*), the "subject" (*grāhaka*) is established; based on the appearance (*nimitta-bhāga*), the "object" (*grāhya*) is established.
As soon as subject and object are complete, the notions of self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*) arise in mutual dependence.

Some maintain that function (*vṛtti*) is the subject-aspect (*lakṣaṇa*) and substance (*svabhāva*) is the object-aspect (*lakṣya*); others hold that the seven consciousnesses are the subject-aspect and the eighth consciousness is the object-aspect. Consequently, they all falsely grasp at real selves and phenomena upon these two aspects of perception and appearance. Since these two grasps are non-existent, one falsely imagines the existence of external selves and phenomena beyond these two aspects of perception and appearance; because all such things are non-existent, everything is *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). This "only" negates the existence of objects, while "consciousness" excludes the emptiness of the mind.

The word "only" (*kevala*) negates the Sarvāstivāda tenet that external objects exist as real entities apart from the mind; the word "consciousness" (*vijñapti*) excludes the views of Bhāviveka and others who misapprehend emptiness, thereby refuting the two extremes of existence and non-existence and correctly abiding in the Middle Way.
Furthermore, according to the explanations of various masters, there are generally four categories of meaning:

first, the aspect of characteristics (*lakṣaṇabhāga*); second, the real characteristic (*lakṣaṇatattva*), which is named "characteristic" because its essence is *tathatā* (suchness), as it is the true characteristic.
2. The name-phase of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-nimitta-nāma-lakṣaṇa*): because it serves as the object for the sense faculties and the mind.
3. The name-phase of characteristics (*ākāra-nimitta-nāma-lakṣaṇa*): this refers exclusively to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), because they possess specific characteristics.
Both the images and the objects are exclusively transformations of consciousness.
Fourth, regarding the "characteristics of meaning" and the "characteristics of names," these refer to the objective portions (viṣayabhāga) of the meanings signified by the expressive words below.
Among these four aspects, the latter three are taken as the objective aspect (nimittabhāga).
Furthermore, the objective aspect is twofold:
first, that which is suddenly transformed by consciousness, which is the primary essence (maulika-bimba).

Regarding the two consciousnesses and so forth that take objects as conditions, they only perceive by transforming into images and do not apprehend the actual essence. As for the second, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"With respect to its own object of perception, there is the function of discernment; the seeing-part has five categories. First, the seeing that is realization (*sākṣāt-darśana*), which refers to the seeing-part of the three fundamental wisdoms."

Second, that which has the function of illuminating is called "seeing" (*darśana*), because this applies to both the faculty (*indriya*) and the mind (*citta*), as both possess the quality of illumination.
Third, that which is capable of cognizing is called "seeing," because all three internal factors (*antaranga-traya*) are equally capable of cognition.
Fourth, conceptual discernment (vitarka) is called "view" because it is that which defines the meaning expressed by the mind.
Fifth, inferential deliberation (vicāra) is called "view" because it is the mental state of inference that deliberates upon all objects.

Among these five aspects of cognition (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), with the exception of the five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) and the two divisions of internal and external [objects], all others are subsumed under the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*).

Third, the aspect of self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*): this refers to that which can directly realize its own aspect of seeing and correctly cognize the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), thereby functioning as the realization itself.

Fourth, the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*): this refers to that which can directly cognize the third aspect, the self-cognizing aspect, because it is non-erroneous in taking the seeing aspect as its object.
It is named according to that which it cognizes.

Regarding the meaning of these four parts: the mirror-like nature is like the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*); the clarity of the mirror is like the seeing part (*darśana-bhāga*); the images in the mirror are like the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*); and the handle at the back of the mirror is like the verifying-of-self-verifying part (*svasaṃvedana-saṃvedana-bhāga*).
Regarding these four parts, there are four masters who establish their respective doctrines.
First, the Bodhisattva Sthiramati establishes one part, the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"This self-verifying portion (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) arises from its object of cognition (ālambana); because it is dependently originated (paratantra-svabhāva), it is said to exist.
The two portions—the seeing and the characterized—do not arise from conditions; they exist due to the false attachment of the mind of universal imagination (parikalpa)."
Thus, these two parts [the object-apprehending and self-cognizing] exist in sentiment but lack rational basis.
Only the self-verifying part (svasaṃvittibhāga) is of the nature of dependence on others (paratantrasvabhāva); because it arises from seeds and is substantially existent.

The two parts—the perceived and the perceiving—are non-existent; furthermore, the transformation that gives rise to the dual grasping at self and phenomena is also non-existent, because what is non-existent resembles non-existence.
According to the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, however, this is a case of what is existent resembling non-existence.
The two aspects—the seeing and the perceived—are substantial;
the transformation that gives rise to the two attachments to self and phenomena is without substance.
Therefore, Sthiramati quotes the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, saying:

"Because it is said that 'the contaminated minds and mental factors of the three realms all have false conceptualization as their intrinsic nature,' we know that the seeing and image aspects of the eight consciousnesses are all falsely grasped as existing through pervasive imagination."
"Only that single portion which is self-cognized (svasaṃvedana) is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), because it is substantially existent.
Second, the master Nanda established that consciousness-only consists of two portions.
First, regarding the statement of the fundamental tenet: all arising moments of mind possess both the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) and the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
These two aspects, the subjective and the objective, constitute the dual conditions of the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*).
If there were no image-part (*nimittabhāga*) to draw forth the mind, mental factors would have no basis for arising;
if there were no perceiving seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*), who would know that there is an objectified image-part?
Thus, with the presence of objects and the presence of mind, the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) is established.

The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is the transformer, while the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) is that which is transformed; for the establishment of the subject-object relationship, both parts must be present.
The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) constitute the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

At times they take an object consisting solely of a mental projection (*pratibimba*), arising from the same seed; at other times they take an object that carries a substantial reality (*sadravya*), arising from different seeds; therefore, they are not the imagined nature (*parikalpita*).
If this were not admitted, the Buddhas would not manifest various images such as their bodies and lands.
Third, the Bodhisattva Dignāga established three parts, while Sthiramati established one part;
[the latter] possesses only the essence but lacks the function.
The establishment of the seen-part (*dṛśya-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) by Nanda consists merely of their function and lacks substantiality; both are mutually deficient.
To "establish a principle" means to establish the meaning of the result of the syllogism (*pramāṇaphala*).
The treatise states:

Because the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), the object of cognition (*prameya*), and the result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) are distinct, and because the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) must necessarily have a substratum upon which they depend;

the image-part is taken as the object of cognition, the seeing-part as the means of cognition, and it is the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) that serves as the cognizer, which is the result of cognition.

It is like using a measuring ruler to measure silk: the silk is the object measured, the ruler is the means of measurement, and the cognition that records the count is called the fruit of measurement.
Now, the fact that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the perceived-image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) do not err is entirely due to the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) acting as the fruit.

Now, when the objective aspect (darśana-bhāga) of visual consciousness perceives blue, it necessarily does not perceive yellow, just as the objective aspect cannot perceive an object never before seen.
When it suddenly perceives a yellow object, it necessarily does not perceive blue; if there were no self-cognizing aspect (svasaṃvitti-bhāga), the objective aspect would be unable to remember itself.
Therefore, one must establish three parts.
If the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) did not exist, then both the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) would also not exist.
If one asserts that there are two parts, then it must necessarily be admitted that the self-verifying part exists.
The *Pramāṇasamuccaya* verse states:
"The object of cognition is the appearance resembling the external object; self-awareness is the aspect of the grasper.
The commentary explains:
"The object of cognition, which resembles the aspect of the object," refers to the image-aspect (nimittabhāga) appearing as if it were an external object.
"The self-awareness of the aspect that is the grasper" refers to the seeing-aspect (darśanabhāga) which grasps the image-aspect.
Therefore, self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is itself the essence.
Fourth, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla establishes four divisions. Regarding the establishment of the thesis:
if one makes a subtle analysis of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), there should be four divisions.

Regarding the establishment of the logical principle: if there were no fourth member [of the syllogism], with what dharma would one establish the third member as the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*)?

You, Dignāga, who established three members, do so because you see that the subjective aspect (*grāhakākāra*) possesses the function of cognizing an object; therefore, you take the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvittikāra*) as the result of valid cognition.

Since your own self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti*) also possesses the capacity to cognize and illuminate its object, what dharma must then be taken as the result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) for that self-cognizing part which serves as the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
It must be that the fourth part, the self-cognition of self-cognition (*svasaṃvittisaṃvitti*), is taken as the result of cognition for the third part.
The *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states: "The mind of sentient beings has two natures:

all internal and external aspects are divided such that one part is the first nature, while the dual division of the seeing (*darśana*) and the appearing (*nimitta*) is the second nature. These are the two natures of the internal and external mind and objects. That which is entangled by the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), and which moves as the active perceiver, is the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the perceiver; that which is grasped is the bondage of the appearing-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*). Because the various distinctions of the seeing-aspect pervade the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is said to be 'various distinctions.'"
Now, that which constitutes a result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) must be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); only then can it be a result of valid cognition.

Although the first five consciousnesses and the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness are indeed direct perceptions, because they take external objects as their conditions, they are not results of valid cognition.
To be the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), it must be an internal object-condition (*ālambana*).
Although the seven consciousnesses are internal object-conditions, they are not the fruit of valid cognition.
To be the fruit of valid cognition, it must possess two characteristics:
First, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); second, internal cognition (*antarālambana*).

Furthermore, although the subsequently attained seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) within the fruit is a form of direct perception, when it internally cognizes its object, it takes a transformed image as its condition; therefore, it is not the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
It must necessarily possess three characteristics.

Furthermore, although the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the fundamental wisdom within the fruit directly realizes suchness, because it does not manifest a mental image (*nimitta*) and is a function of the mind, it is not the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*).
It must be that the essence of mind itself possesses four characteristics:

first, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); second, internal cognition; third, not manifesting a reflected image; and fourth, being the essence of mind—only then does it constitute the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
Question:
"What constitutes the essential nature of the *Caturvargika*? Answer:
"The aspect of the object (*nimittabhāga*) has the transformed matter and mind as its essential nature.
As for the three internal aspects, they take the currently functioning mental factors (*caitta*) as their essence.
*Zhongjing* (Mirror of the School): "Question:"
"Never has there been a mind without an object, nor has there ever been a mind without an object.
Discussing both ordinary beings and sages together, how many objects are there in total? Answer:
"Roughly speaking, there are three types of objects.
The verse says:

'The objective realm (svabhāva-viṣaya) does not follow the mind; its nature is the real meaning. It consists of the actual sense organs and objects, the four great elements, and the objective aspects (nimitta-bhāga) such as the matter produced by meditative concentration.'"

Regarding the statement that "it does not follow the mind": this is because the various aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) such as the sense faculties and their objects are all produced from their own real seeds, and do not arise following the seeds of the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*). "Solitary images" (*kevala-pratibimba*) arise solely from the shadow of the perceiving aspect; "shadow" (*pratibimba*) is a synonym for the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).

Because these are merely provisional objective parts (nimittabhāga) that lack seeds as their accompaniment and exist only nominally, they are called "solitary shadows" (*ekacchāyā*). They are like empty flowers or the horns of a rabbit, and consist of all provisional images and dharmas of the past and future.

This [image] arises solely from the transformation of the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) of the perceiving consciousness; because it is of the same seed as the seeing-part, it is called "solitary-shadow" (tuying) and "arising only from the seeing-part. As for the "image with substance" (dai-zhi), it pertains to both the objective (qing) and the fundamental (ben), that is, the image-part (nimitta-bhāga). One half of it arises from the same seed as the fundamental substance, and the other half arises from the same seed as the seeing-part; therefore, it is said to "pertain to both the objective and the fundamental."

The "affective" (qing) is the perceiving aspect (darśana-bhāga), while the "object" (xiang) is the essential nature (svabhāva) that serves as the focal point; the categories of "nature-seeds" (xingzhong) and so forth are not fixed, meaning they apply respectively to each of the three types of objects as appropriate.
"There is the realm of the seed-nature (*gotra-dhātu*), which is bound to the three aggregates and is indeterminate in its distinctions such as maturation (*vipāka*).
Furthermore, the extensive explanation states:
"As for the objective sphere of nature (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), it is called the objective sphere of nature because it possesses a real substance and its own distinct aspect (*svalakṣaṇa*)."
That is to say, the first five consciousnesses, the eighth mind-king (*citta-rāja*), and the sixth consciousness when it functions as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—

when these take real matter (*rūpa*) as their object and apprehend the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of that object without being accompanied by names or concepts, and without the mind engaging in deliberation— only then is such an object termed a "nature-object" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).

Furthermore, when fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) takes True Suchness (tathatā) as its object, it is also an objective realm (svabhāva-viṣaya), because it functions spontaneously and without conceptual discrimination (nirvikalpa).
Regarding the statement "not following the mind," there are five kinds of non-following: first, non-following in terms of nature (svabhāva).

While its subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga), which acts as the perceiver, may pertain to all three natures (tri-svabhāva), its objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga), which is the perceived object, is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta); thus, it does not follow the subjective aspect in its capacity to pertain to all three natures.

2. Regarding "the seeds do not follow": this means that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) arises from its own seed as a seeing-part, and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) arises from its own seed as an image-part; because they do not arise from the seeds of the mind that constitutes the seeing-part which acts as the objective support (*ālambaka*), it is called "seeds do not follow."

Third, regarding those that do not follow the realm-affiliation (*dhātu-bandhana*): for example, when the clearly manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes fragrance or taste as its objects, these two objects—fragrance and taste—are bound exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and thus do not follow the clearly manifest mental consciousness, which extends to the higher realms.

Furthermore, when the eighth consciousness of the desire realm takes seeds as its object, that which acts as the perceiver—the eighth consciousness—is bound exclusively to the desire realm, whereas the seeds that are its objects pertain to all three realms; thus, between the sixth and eighth consciousnesses, there is a lack of correspondence regarding their respective realm-attachments.

Fourth, regarding the non-inclusion within the three categories (*tri-nikāya*): first, concerning non-inclusion within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the five consciousnesses is subsumed under the seed of consciousness, while the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the five objects is included within the aggregate of form; thus, it is not included in the category of aggregates.

Regarding non-inclusion within the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), the seeing-part of the five consciousnesses is subsumed under the mind-base (*mana-āyatana*), while the image-part of the five objects is included within the five objective bases; thus, it is not included in the category of bases.

Regarding non-inclusion within the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), the seeing-part of the five consciousnesses is subsumed under the five consciousness-elements, while the image-part of the five objects is included within the five objective elements; this constitutes non-inclusion within the three categories.

Fifth, regarding "the maturation not following [its object]": this refers to the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) of the eighth consciousness, which is of the nature of maturation (*vipāka-svabhāva*), while its perceived objects—the five dust-like image-parts (*nimitta-bhāga*)—are not of the nature of maturation; this is termed "the maturation not following."

Regarding the "object of solitary shadow" (*ekacchāyālambana*): it refers to the case where the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) arise from the same seed, and thus it is called "solitary shadow," being exclusively derived from the seeing-part.

This includes, for example, when the sixth consciousness takes as its object empty flowers, rabbit horns, the past or future, or transforms an image to take as its object the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); as well as taking as its object dharmas of the earth element, or taking as its object the fruits of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the extremely remote (*atidūra*), or the extremely subtle (*atisūkṣma*). All such cases are merely false images.
These arise solely from the transformation of the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) and possess no seeds of their own; thus they are said to "arise solely from the seeing.
There are two types of solitary images (*kevala-chāyā*):

first, solitary images without a real substrate (*nirvastuka*), which are the objective-images (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by the sixth consciousness when it takes such things as empty flowers, rabbit horns, or the past and future as its objects.
Its *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) arises from the same seed as the sixth *darśana-bhāga* (perceptual aspect), and lacks a real substrate such as a flower in the sky.

Second is the "solitary image with a substrate," which refers to the sixth consciousness taking the seeds and manifestations of the five sense organs as its object; because these all arise by relying upon a substrate, their *nimitta-bhāga* also arises from the same seed as the *darśana-bhāga*, and this is also termed a "solitary-image object."
Third, regarding those with a substantial basis (*sapratiṣṭha*): this refers to when the mind takes the mind itself as its object.

For example, when the seventh consciousness takes the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its object, its image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) does not arise from a separate seed; rather, one half arises from the same seed as the substantial basis, and the other half arises from the same seed as the seeing-portion that acts as the perceiver.
That which arises from its own essence is of an unobscured nature;
that which arises from the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) of the cognitive faculty is of an obscured nature.
Because it encompasses both ends of the spectrum of indeterminate states, it is termed "pervading both the mental concomitants and the essence."

The "substantial" (zhi) refers to the seventh consciousness's subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) which acts as the cognizer; the "original" (ben) refers to the eighth consciousness's objective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) which serves as the object.
Furthermore, according to the fourfold classification, that which is exclusively of a distinct seed and not of a common seed is the "nature-object" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).
Second, those that are exclusively of the same kind and not of different kinds, namely the object of "solitary shadow" (duoying-jing).
Third, the category of "both," namely the object of "carrying substance" (dai zhi-jing).
Fourth, the category of "neither," namely the fundamental wisdom (benzhi) taking suchness (rú) as its object.
Because True Suchness (tathatā) does not arise from the seeds of the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga), it is called "not of the same seed.

Furthermore, because the essence of True Suchness itself is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and is realized only through its manifestation, rather than being a phenomenon produced by productive causes, it is called "not of a distinct seed."
Regarding "the nature-seed and so forth according to their respective applications": "nature" refers to the objective realm (*viṣaya*), and "various" refers to the different types.
This means that within each of the three objects, there are distinct categories; all of these must now be explained according to their respective applications.

Furthermore, if distinguished according to the eight consciousnesses, the first five evolving consciousnesses are at all times exclusively *xing-jing* (objective realms of their own nature), regardless of whether they function interchangeably or not.
Among the two types of transformation, it is only the transformation through causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-pariṇāma*), and because it shares the same objects as the five sense faculties.
The sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has four categories:

first, the clear and distinct consciousness (*vibhāvaka-manovijñāna*), which also encompasses the three types of objects; when it perceives the actual five sensory objects in common with the five faculties, in the initial moment of sudden encounter (*ābhoga-citta*), this is an objective realm (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).

If a subsequent thought takes as its object the provisional forms—such as square, round, long, or short—within the five sense-objects, it constitutes a "solitary shadow" (duoying) with substance; this is also termed a "seemingly substantial" (sidadizhi) object.

Second, the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in the state of distraction also encompasses all three types of objects; it is mostly a solitary shadow, as it universally takes as its objects dharmas of the three periods of time, whether they possess substance or lack substance.
When taking as an object one's own currently functioning mind and mental factors, it is an object that carries a substance (sābhāsaviṣaya).

When taking as an object one's own five sense faculties, or taking as an object the minds and mental factors of another person, it is an object consisting of a mere shadow (pratibimba-mātra-viṣaya), which is also called an object resembling one that carries a substance.

Furthermore, the independent manovijñāna (solitary mental consciousness), in its first moment, takes the five sense objects as its object; when it takes a portion of actual matter (*bhūtarūpa*) as its object, this is also called a "real object" (*svabhāvaviṣaya*).

Third, the manovijñāna within meditative concentration also encompasses all three types of objects; because it universally takes as its objects dharmas of both substantial and insubstantial nature throughout the three periods of time, these are "solely reflected images" (*kevalapratibimba-viṣaya*).
Furthermore, because it can take as its object the currently functioning mind and mental factors within one's own continuum, it is an "object with substance" (*sadravya-viṣaya*).

Moreover, prior to the seventh stage, even during states of meditative concentration that involve outflows (*sāsrava*), it is capable of inducing the five consciousnesses to perceive the five sense objects; thus, it is a "real object" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).
Fourth, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in dreams perceives only "solitary-shadow" objects (*kevala-pratibimba-viṣaya*).

The seventh consciousness perceives only "substantially-associated" objects (*sadravya-sambandha-viṣaya*). As for the eighth consciousness, its primary mind-king (*citta-rāja*) perceives only "objective-nature" objects (*mūla-vastu-viṣaya*), because it undergoes transformation through causes and conditions; the five associated mental factors (*caitasika*), such as attention (*manasikāra*), are "pseudo-substantially-associated," which is to say, they are "true solitary-shadow" objects.
Question:
"What constitutes the substance of the three objects? Answer:
"First, regarding the nature and object (*svabhāva-viṣaya*): its substance consists of the five real sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), as it is constituted by eight factors (*aṣṭa-dharma*).
These eight factors are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)—earth, water, fire, and wind—and the four subtle qualities (*tanmātra*)—form, odor, taste, and tangibility."

Speaking in terms of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), if one considers those [consciousnesses] that take contaminated states (*sāsrava*) as their objects—excluding the seventh consciousness—all other seven [consciousnesses] have their own mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) as their substance.

Regarding the second type, the "solely imagined object" (*kevala-vikalpa-gocara*), its substance consists of the provisional aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the sixth consciousness; the perceiving subject itself has its own mind and mental factors as its substance.
The third is the "object-included" (saviṣaya), which takes as its essence the provisional aspect (nimitta-bhāga) that arises through transformation;
if it functions within the state of being with outflows (sāsrava), it takes as its essence only the mind and mental factors of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"Traveling afar and wandering alone, bodiless and reclining in the cave, one who tames the mind that is difficult to tame—such a person is called a true brahmin."
The *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra-vyākhyā* states:

"The Tathāgata, relying on the locus of the mental faculty (*manas*), speaks of 'far-reaching' and 'solitary travel. Because it follows along with the ignorance-consciousness (*avidyā-manovijñāna*) as it universally perceives all objects, it is called 'far-reaching.'"
Furthermore, because each moment in the continuity of the mind arises in succession, there is no real sovereign; thus it is called "acting alone.
That which is "without body" means that the mind has no physical form or substance.
"To sleep in the cave" means that [the mind] relies upon the various sense-faculties and secretly turns within the body; this is called "sleeping in the cave.
"Sleeping" (mai) means "to store" (zang).
It refers to the mind being stored within the body.
The intent of this verse is to refute the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) attachment to a real self (*ātman*).
The World-Honored One said:
"It is only the mind that wanders alone; there is no separate sovereign controller. Therefore, it is called "wandering alone."
"Furthermore, because it has wandered through the realms of the six sense objects since beginningless time, it is called 'Far-Reaching' (dūramgamā).
[Amala] is translated here as "Pure Consciousness.
Sengdun’s commentary on the *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra* states:
"The pure and stainless consciousness.
Regarding this, the Buddha said in that sutra:
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, always transform all consciousnesses through a single awakening, causing them to enter the *amala* [consciousness]."
Why is this? Because all sentient beings possess original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

[The Buddha] constantly uses this single awakening to awaken all sentient beings, causing them all to attain original enlightenment and to realize that all sensory consciousnesses are empty, quiescent, and unarisen.
"Why is this? Because the determined nature is fundamentally without movement. The *Xunwen* says:
"Tiantai, relying on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, explains that amala is called the light of non-discriminative wisdom; it is precisely the ninth pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*).
The *Zhongjing* states:

Regarding the five Buddha-eyes:
I shall first provide a general exposition and subsequently clarify them individually.
As for the general exposition, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"When a bodhisattva practices prajñā, they purify the five eyes.
The flesh eye is purified, seeing the trichiliocosm;
the divine eye is purified, seeing the deaths and births of sentient beings within the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The Bodhisattva Wisdom-Eye does not form such thoughts as:
"This dharma is conditioned or unconditioned, mundane or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows."

This Bodhisattva of the Wisdom-Eye does not fail to see any dharma, does not fail to know any dharma, and does not fail to recognize any dharma; this is what it means for a Bodhisattva to have the purity of the Wisdom-Eye.

With the Dharma-eye, one knows that this person enters the stage of following through faith, this person follows through the Dharma, this person practices the signless, this person practices the liberation door of emptiness, this person practices the liberation door of the signless, and this person practices the liberation door of wishlessness, thereby attaining the five eyes.
Because he attains the five eyes, he attains the uninterrupted samādhi (*ānantarya-samādhi*).
Because he attains the uninterrupted samādhi, he attains the wisdom of liberation, and so forth. ...
up to knowing whether this bodhisattva is able to sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) or is unable to sit at the site of enlightenment.
Knowing whether this bodhisattva has Māra or is free from Māra constitutes the pure Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva. Maudgalyāyana said to Māra:
"I observe the interior with my eye of the Way and behold the exterior with my divine eye; both inside and out are pure, surpassing celestial lapis lazuli."
When a bodhisattva enters the vajra-like samādhi, they shatter all afflictions and habitual tendencies; immediately, they attain the unimpeded liberation of all Buddhas, and the Buddha-eye is born.

That which is called the knowledge of all modes, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and even the various merits such as great loving-kindness and great compassion—this is termed the Buddha-eye.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains:

"The fleshly eye sees what is near but not what is distant; it sees what is in front but not what is behind; it sees what is external but not what is internal; it sees by day but not at night; and it sees what is above but not what is below."

Because of these obstructions, one seeks the divine eye; having attained this divine eye, one sees both far and near, before and behind, inside and outside, by day and night, above and below—all without obstruction. This is what is seen by the divine eye.
Conditioned phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions and are merely provisional designations; their true nature is not perceived.
That is to say, they are empty, signless, wishless, unarisen, and unceasing; as it is before, so it is in the middle and at the end. For the sake of this true nature, one seeks the eye of wisdom.

To attain the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) by not seeing sentient beings, to completely extinguish the marks of unity and difference, to abandon all attachments, and to not grasp at any phenomena—wherein wisdom itself is extinguished within—is called the wisdom-eye.
However, the wisdom-eye cannot deliver sentient beings.
Why is this? Because it is free from all conceptual discrimination.
For this reason, the Dharma-eye arises.

This Dharma-eye enables the practitioner to practice this Dharma, attain this Path, and know the various skillful means for each and every sentient being, leading them to realize the attainment of the Path.
The Dharma-eye cannot universally know the skillful means for delivering sentient beings; for this reason, one seeks the Buddha-eye.
The Buddha-eye knows nothing it does not perceive: though obstructions may be dense, there is nothing it does not see and know.
What is extremely distant for others is near to the Buddha;
what is obscure for others is luminous to the Buddha;
what is a matter of doubt for others is certain for the Buddha.
What is subtle for others is coarse for the Buddha;
what is profound for others is shallow for the Buddha.
For the Buddha’s eye, there is nothing it does not hear, nothing it does not see, nothing it does not know, nothing that is difficult, and nothing requiring deliberation.
"Among all dharmas, the Buddha-eye constantly illumines them.
Regarding these five eyes, four meanings should be established to distinguish their characteristics.
First, they are categorized according to persons; as the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā* states:
"If one intends to refer to humans, this refers to the fleshly eye; since the eyes of the four miserable realms do not equal those of humans and devas, [the former] are what are refuted.

This is also a general rule, for there are also dragons and ghosts whose fleshly eyes surpass those of humans; however, they are ultimately categorized as such based on their evil karma and their departure from the Path."
It is further said:
"Because the dharma of the divine eye (divyacakṣus) exists within the realm of form (rūpadhātu), it is only after transcending desire that the four dhyānas and the divine eye arise.

The śrāvaka possesses the wisdom-eye (prajñācakṣus); this is the wisdom-eye I have attained since the past. The bodhisattva possesses the dharma-eye (dharmacakṣus), and the Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye (buddhacakṣus)."
*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā*: Question:
"The first three eyes can also be attained by the two vehicles of the two teachings.
The Dharma-eye can also be attained by bodhisattvas of the three teachings."
"How can it be that the five eyes are all collectively denied as non-existent?
He replied:
"In accordance with the teachings and based on principle, their characteristics differ according to the realm."
If it is said that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess [the four eyes], these are the four eyes as endowed with principle (*li*).

While they are partially attained during the stages and abodes (*bhūmi-vihāra*), they are only perfected by the Buddha; therefore, it is said that the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) perceives the ten directions all at once, and the heavenly eye (*divya-cakṣus*) perceives without the duality of marks (*nimitta*).
Because the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus) is said to be the foremost purity, the Dharma-eye (dharma-cakṣus) and the Buddha-eye (buddha-cakṣus) are fundamentally and eternally distinct.
Thus, the five eyes are fully possessed by the Buddha alone;
since those of the two vehicles and ordinary humans lack these eyes altogether, they are like those born blind.
Question:
"What is the difference between the Buddha’s physical eye and the physical eyes of ordinary people? Answer:
"Ordinary beings are like the blind due to the obstructions of their evil karma, whereas they are purified by the permeation of the meritorious qualities of the Buddha-fruit.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
'The Buddha’s physical eye can see countless worlds among human realms, not merely those within the range of his sensory obstructions.'"
"Therefore, know that the ordinary person's fleshly eye sees only what is within its range of obstruction; by definition, it is like being blind. He asked:
"Since the fleshly eye is obstructed, how can it see everywhere?"
Answer: The *Mahā-śāstra* states:
"The celestial eye born of retribution is situated within the physical eye."
"The celestial eye is opened and the physical eye perceives forms; therefore, one sees the great trichiliocosm.
It further states:
"The celestial eye is of two kinds:"
There are two ways of obtaining [the divine eye]: first, by way of karmic retribution; second, by way of practicing dhyāna.
That obtained through karmic retribution is always used in conjunction with the fleshly eye, whereas the divine eye alone is used specifically in the darkness of night.
Question: "The Buddha possesses the fleshly eye (māṃsacakṣus) and the Buddha-eye (buddhacakṣus); what are their similarities and differences? Answer:
The *Vimalakīrti Commentary* states:
"The Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Dharma-body Bodhisattvas differ in five aspects when distinguished by way of essence and function.
For instance, when the fleshly eye perceives coarse forms, it perceives the Middle Way within those coarse forms."
"From the perspective of coarse form, it is called the fleshly eye;
in terms of seeing the Middle Way, it is called the Buddha-eye. Question:
"What is the difference between the Buddha’s divine eye (divyacakṣus) and the Buddha’s wisdom-eye (buddhacakṣus)?
Answer: "The *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā* states:"
"Now, to realize the principle and perceive the coarse and subtle forms of the lands of the ten directions and the ten dharma realms is called the Buddha’s divine eye (divyacakṣus).
To see the three truths as perfectly non-dual is called the Buddha’s eye (buddhacakṣus)."
Second, the explanation by way of function, as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā*:
"The eye is merely a general name; when distinguished according to its functions, there are five kinds:
first, the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), which sees coarse material forms."
2. The divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) sees subtle forms that are the results and causes [of karma];
3. The wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*) sees the principle of partial truth regarding coarse and subtle forms and mind;
4. The dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) sees all dharmas of conventional truth, which are the provisional names for the causes and conditions of coarse and subtle forms and mind.

Fifth, the Buddha-eye perceives the principle of the Middle Way, the perfect and true Buddha-nature, and is further able to simultaneously illumine both the coarse and subtle aspects of the phenomena and principles of dependent origination.
Question:

"If perceiving the truth of the Middle Way is called the Buddha-eye, I do not yet understand the similarities and differences between the partial realization of a Bodhisattva and the ultimate realization of a Buddha."
Answer: As stated in the *Fazhen*:
"The five eyes of partial realization and those of ultimate perfection differ only in terms of clarity and obscurity."
3. Explanation by way of the Truths (*satya*): As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*:
"To contemplate the three truths in their perfection—contemplating the conventional realm and destroying all evil karma—is called 'purifying the fleshly eye.'"
Contemplating the subtle objects of conventional reality to destroy all distracted minds is called the pure divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Contemplating ultimate truth to destroy the afflictions within the realms is called the pure wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*).
Observing both the internal and external conventional realms, shattering the sands of ignorance, is called the pure Dharma-eye.
Observing the middle with dual illumination, perfectly eliminating ignorance, is the pure Buddha-eye.
These, then, are the two eyes—the fleshly eye and the heavenly eye—which are dharmas produced through causes and conditions;
the latter three are the truths illuminated by the three contemplations.
Regarding the fourth [eye], the explanation according to the teachings is as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*:
"According to the teaching by way of compendium, there are differences regarding the four Buddhas and the five eyes.
In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha asked Subhūti:
"Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? [And so forth...]"
According to this, all five eyes pertain to the four teachings.
To explain them individually, the *Vimalakīrti-ṭīkā* states:
"If one distinguishes between the partial and the perfect in their mutual relation, and explains them collectively, there is only the Buddha-eye of the Perfect [Teaching]."
The distinct teaching is the Dharma-eye;
it is common to the Bodhisattva’s wisdom-eye;
and it contains the Bodhisattva’s two eyes: the flesh-eye and the divine-eye.
Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states:
"If ordinary beings possess the fleshly eye and the divine eye, they perceive coarse and subtle forms.
Śrāvakas, however, possess only three eyes:"
The physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) and the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) see as previously described;
the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) sees the characteristics of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is itself the seeing of the characteristics of the two truths.

Since a *piṭaka-traya* bodhisattva has not yet severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), they do not see the characteristics of ultimate truth, but possess only the physical and divine eyes that perceive the coarse characteristics of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) likewise possess only the three eyes, perceiving only the illusory manifestations of the two truths.
The Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) attain the four eyes.

Three eyes are as previously described; they additionally attain the Dharma-eye (dharmacakṣus), by which they perceive the sands-of-the-Ganges teachings of the Buddhas within and beyond the realms, as well as the principles of the immeasurable Four Truths—all of which constitute the perception of both the noumenon and its phenomena.

If a Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) dwells in the stage of the Ten Faiths, although they possess only the physical eye (māṃsa-cakṣus), it is called the Buddha-eye; they have a semblance of the perfect vision of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Yet, because delusions regarding appearances have not been eliminated, this is still termed "the seeing of appearances."
"If one enters the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) and gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), the five eyes will then open perfectly; this is a general explanation.
Next, to explain specifically, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra Commentary* quotes the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which says:
"What did Aniruddha say? [The text continues: "Aniruddha said:"
"When I first left the household life, I was constantly fond of sleep, and the Tathāgata rebuked me as being of the same class as animals.
Upon hearing the Buddha's rebuke, I wept and reproached myself; I did not sleep for seven days, and consequently lost both my eyes. I went to the Buddha and recounted this in detail."
The Buddha said:

"Sleep is the nutriment of the eyes. Just as a person who does not eat for seven days will lose their life, so too the life of the eyes is severed if one does not sleep for seven days; it is difficult to treat such a condition."
"One should cultivate the divine eye (divyacakṣus) in order to perceive worldly affairs.
Consequently, by practicing dhyāna, one attains the four great pure forms (catvāri mahābhūtāni rūpāṇi viśuddhāni), which allow one to see with half the head.
Regarding what is called "half the head," the ancient Shenwu said:
"The upper half of the brow is as clear and transparent as lapis lazuli.
This contradicts the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which describes clarity in front but not behind.
Nanping said:
"The front half of his head sees the great trichiliocosm; he sees only what is before him and not what is behind.
Now, this interpretation contradicts the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, which states:
"When Nālada cultivates dhyāna, he attains the pure derived matter of the four great elements as a 'half-head celestial eye'; from the upper half of his head, he is able to see all forms."

One contemplates the trichiliocosm as if it were an *āmala* fruit; if one is a Buddha of the Tripitaka, having attained the divine eye of a whole head, the pure color emanates from the entire head, seeing through all things without obstruction.
"Now, observing these two views, they are like the heron and the clam clutching one another.
We shall now take advantage of this juncture to harmonize them through comprehensive integration.
When the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* extensively explains that taking the higher [stages] constitutes the 'half,' it is revealing the essence of the divine eye."
The celestial eye obtained as a karmic retribution exists within the physical eye;
the celestial eye obtained through cultivation exists outside the physical eye.
Since it is outside the eye, it manifests a color that covers half the head.
Although it is half the head that is purified, when viewing objects, one sees only what is before them.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* explains this in terms of its functional application.
Nevertheless, there is a vast difference in quality between the divine eye produced by a Śrāvaka, which occupies half the head, and that of a Buddha, which occupies the entire head.
Furthermore, the Buddha can see whatever he wishes to see simply by entering the corresponding meditative absorption;
the Śrāvakas, however, must enter the specific absorption they have attained before they can perceive an object.
Moreover, the Buddha is able to see all buddha-fields, whereas Nārada sees only the trichiliocosm.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states:
"Although those of the Two Vehicles possess the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), they must apply deliberate attention (*manasikāra*) to see a thousand worlds or even a great trichiliocosm.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess the true divine eye; they do not perceive the Buddha-fields through dualistic characteristics."
Tiantai said:
"The true celestial eye of the Middle Way does not possess the characteristics of the two truths;

yet it is able to universally illumine the four lands and the three kinds of birth-and-death, wherein one dies here and is born there, with both the primary and secondary realms appearing simultaneously."
Within the King Samādhi, this is the true divine eye.
Question:
"If Nanda had already seen it before him, why did he ask another person to help thread the needle?"
He replied:
"One sees [them] when entering meditative concentration, but does not know [them] upon emerging from it.
Zhaò said:
"The two vehicles see [the Buddha] when they are in meditative concentration, but do not see him when they emerge from it.
Jingxi’s *Commentary* states:
"If we consider the case of Nanda losing his eyesight, then upon emerging from contemplation, he would simply be like ordinary people whose faculties are impaired and thus unable to see."
Question: "Since the two teachings of the Tripiṭaka and the Shared Vehicle do not discuss the Middle Way, what constitutes the Buddha-eye? Answer:
The *Biexing Xuanki* states:

"Therefore, now the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and the two types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are exhausted simultaneously; thus, one is able to bring both truths (*satya*) to ultimate fulfillment."
"This distinguishes them from the disciples of the three vehicles, uniquely manifesting the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom.
Furthermore, although the divine eye of Nalakalpa and that of the Great Brahma King are similar, upon examination there are four differences:
first, the difference between retribution and cultivation; the Brahma King’s is obtained through retribution and resides within the physical eye.
The attainment cultivated by Nanda is situated outside of the fleshly eye.
Second, the distinction between the general and the specific.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states:
Furthermore, the Brahma King perceives through general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), and thus his vision is not distinct;
Aniruddha perceives through specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), and thus his vision is clear and precise.
This extends to all Arhats who have attained [vision] through pure dhyāna; they all perceive through specific characteristics.
Third, the distinction between self and others.
The Brahma King’s vision is obtained through retribution; he sees only within his own dwelling place and not in other directions.

Aniruddha, however, by cultivating the fundamental [dhyānas], attained the five types of the four dhyānas and the eightfold purity of form, thereby developing the true divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); wherever he goes, he sees the entire trichiliocosm.
Fourth, the distinction between supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and clear knowledges (*vidyā*): the divine eye of a Brahmā king is a supernormal power but not a clear knowledge;
the divine eye of an Arhat is both a supernormal power and a clear knowledge.
Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* asks:
Question: "The Brahma King’s divine eye perceives the great trichiliocosm; how does this differ from the 'fleshly eye' mentioned in the *Lotus Sūtra*? Answer:
"The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that the divine eye born of retribution resides within the fleshly eye."
The celestial eye is opened and expanded; because it sees broadly by means of the heavenly fleshly eye (māṃsacakṣus), it perceives the great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies that the fleshly eye of a bodhisattva sees for a hundred *yojanas*, and even up to the great trichiliocosm.
Beyond this, one employs the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Because the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) is incompatible with the wind [element], it is not said that it sees other lands.
However, by the power of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the fleshly eye is able to see all phenomena within the great trichiliocosm.
Even the three piṭakas and the two vehicles—with their divine eye and wisdom eye—cannot equal the phenomena and principles they perceive, let alone be compared to the Brahma King.
Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"One who studies the Mahāyāna, though possessing only the fleshly eye, is said to have the Buddha-eye.
Those of the Two Vehicles, though possessing the wisdom-eye, are said to have only the fleshly eye."
With this eye of wisdom, one perceives the truth and severs delusions; thus, it is both equal to and inferior to the physical eye of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
The reason the physical eye of the Perfect Teaching is called the Buddha-eye is that although it possesses the nature of afflictions, it is able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata.
“Śrotra” (娑路多羅戌縷多) means "that which can hear.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Because sound repeatedly reaches the hearing within this [organ], it is translated as 'ear' (*karṇa*); this carries the meaning of 'that which can hear.'"
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"The ear is like a freshly rolled leaf. Some say:
"The ears are like rolled birch bark.
[Kāraṇa-karṇa] means "able to smell.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Because it is by means of this that one is able to smell odors, it is called the nose; 'nose' (nāsā) has the meaning of 'that which smells.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"The nose is like a pair of hanging claws."
Some say: "The nose is like a needle-case.
[The term *ṛśya* (or *ṛśyati*) is pronounced with a stammering sound; this means "capable of tasting," for it can eliminate hunger and thirst.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Because it can eliminate hunger, thirst, and emaciation; because it frequently engages in speech, expresses itself, and calls out, it is named 'tongue' (*jihvā*), which carries the meaning of 'that which tastes.'"
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"The tongue is like the crescent moon, bent downward.
Or it is said:
"The tongue is like a crescent moon blade.
[Kāya]: In Sanskrit, there are four names:
first, kāya; second, śarīra; third, deha; and fourth, aṅga.
This is translated as "accumulation.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Because it is that which is followed by the various faculties and is accumulated throughout, it is called 'body' (*kāya*); this carries the meaning of accumulation, as well as the meaning of being a basis."
It is also translated as "division," meaning a limb or member.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"The body is like the belly of a waist-drum."
Some say: "The body is like a standing halberd.
The *Ānāpāna-smṛti Sūtra* says:
"What is the body? What is the physical form?
The bones and flesh constitute the body;
the union of the six sense organs constitutes the physical form."
“*Hṛdaya*”: this is translated as the "fleshly heart-mass," which is that upon which the faculty of mind (*manas*) relies.
Therefore it is said:
"The mind is like seeing within a dark chamber."
Now, regarding what is called the "root" (indriya), there are two meanings:
first, the external root of the floating-dust; second, the internal root of ultimate reality.
As for the "floating-dust," the four great elements are the creators, and the four subtle particles are the created.
The four subtle elements of form, fragrance, flavor, and touch combine to form the sense organs.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"I now observe these four dust-like elements of the floating roots; they reside only upon my face."
Zizhong said: "Floating and empty, it is unreal; it clouds and obscures the true nature, and is therefore called 'floating dust.
This refers to the external sense organs of floating dust."
Regarding the term "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*), it refers to the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The *Hongmin Chao* states:
"Although these ultimate sense faculties take the eight factors—both the primary creators and their derived products—as their substance, they are invisible."
The capacity of resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) to illuminate objects and give rise to consciousness is the domain known by the noble ones (*ārya*).
Its meaning is profound and far-reaching, unlike the coarse and shallow nature of the sensory realms (*viṣaya*); therefore, it is called "pure" (*śubha*).
This is purity spoken of within the context of defilement; it is not the purity of untainted, wondrous clarity.
This is the internal organ of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks:
"Why is it that the objects known by three consciousnesses are combined into one, such that the olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses are termed 'perception' (saṃjñā);

whereas the objects known by [the other] three consciousnesses are distinguished as three, with the visual termed 'seeing,' the auditory termed 'hearing,' and the mental termed 'cognition' (vijñāna)?"
Answer: "These three consciousnesses have many factors that assist the path; therefore, they are explained separately.
The other three consciousnesses are not so; therefore, they are explained together."
These three consciousnesses cognize only worldly matters; therefore, they are combined into one.
The remaining three consciousnesses cognize both the worldly and the supramundane; therefore, they are explained separately.

Furthermore, these three consciousnesses take only indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena as their objects, whereas the other three consciousnesses may take wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate phenomena as their objects.

Furthermore, these three consciousnesses can produce the causes and conditions for the Three Vehicles; for example, seeing the Buddha and his disciples with the eye, hearing the Dharma with the ear, and the mind’s deliberation and correct mindfulness—such various distinctions as these.
In the *Suvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, the Buddha told the Heavenly King:
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by means of the power of skillful means, practice the prajñā-pāramitā, and thus their minds attain mastery in taking all dharmas as objects."
Taking all forms as an object of focus, they vow to attain the physical form of a Buddha through non-attainment;
taking all sounds as an object of focus, they vow to attain the subtle and wondrous voice of a Tathāgata;
taking all fragrances as an object of focus, they vow to attain the pure fragrance of a Tathāgata’s precepts.
When the mind takes various flavors as its object, one vows to obtain the Tathāgata’s mark of being the foremost great man among those who possess flavors;
when the mind takes various tangibles as its object, one vows to obtain the Tathāgata’s soft palms;
when the mind takes various phenomena as its object, one vows to obtain the Tathāgata’s tranquil mind.
The mind takes its own body as its object, vowing to attain the Buddha-body;
the mind takes its own mouth as its object, vowing to attain the Buddha-mouth;
the mind takes its own mind as its object, vowing to attain the Tathāgata’s impartial mind.
"O Heavenly King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, there is not a single thought or a single action that passes in vain without being directed toward sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)."
Universally taking all phenomena as objects of cognition, yet remaining unattached;
observing all phenomena, there are none that do not tend toward the path to Bodhi.
The various practices cultivated by a Bodhisattva are all established through external conditions.
Furthermore, it is like the great earth resting upon the waters; if one digs a pond or a well, one immediately obtains water for use.
Those who do not dig have no means of seeing it.
In this way, the realm of noble wisdom pervades all phenomena; if one diligently cultivates the skillful means of Prajñā, one will then attain it.
