Among the Bodhisattvas, for the time being, we restrict ourselves to their respective stages and further set aside the sequential entry; therefore, it is not mentioned here, though it would indeed be appropriate according to principle.
Regarding the application of the single principle of the gate, it corresponds to the respective divisions; since this is identical to the application of the Dharma, one employs only this for now.

Furthermore, the single principle of the application of the Dharma also extends to the Esoteric Teachings, wherein one may fully employ all three principles as discussed in the "Expedient Means" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The Six Principles of Confucian poetry take "the absence of deviant thoughts" as their ultimate aim;
the Five Periods of the Buddhist teachings take the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as their final goal.
Truly, this is the supreme assembly of a single transformation and the ultimate pinnacle of all Buddhas; it is like the vast void containing all colors, or like the Bohai Sea receiving all streams.

Thus, like one peering through a tube at the Sky of Meaning or drawing from the Ocean of Dharma with a conch-shell ladle, I have roughly investigated and savored the true exegesis; how could this be of any value to the Great Sages?
First, I shall distinguish the titles of the chapters; second, I shall discuss the meaning of the chapters.
First, regarding the analysis of the chapter title:
the Sūtra states, "After a long time, the Buddhas must speak the truth.
Since the text has already set aside the provisional means, the title should be designated as "The Truth"; why then establish this current chapter under a name of expediency?
It is like hanging a placard on the gate of a prefecture.
Furthermore, when the Buddha arose from his meditative concentration, he himself proclaimed:
"The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable."
This is a double praise of the provisional and the real.
A former master thus remarked:
"If these flowers do not exist, that is one thing; but if they do exist, they contain both flower and fruit."
"If this sutra had not spoken [of these matters], it would have been sufficient; since it does speak of them, it must distinguish both the provisional and the real.
Since the sutra clarifies both the provisional and the real, why does the title single out only the "expedient means" (*upāya*)?
From this doubt arises the succession of past masters, who together established seven meanings to extend the intent of the title.
First, provisional teachings possess the function of revealing the ultimate reality.

When the Dharma King first began his transformation of beings, their capacities and conditions were not yet mature; he thus concealed the ultimate and established the provisional, whereby the provisional obscured the ultimate.
At the wondrous assembly on Vulture Peak, he universally gathered those of the provisional vehicles and definitively resolved the teachings for the śrāvakas—this is the king of all sutras.

That which was previously concealed has now been revealed and perfected as the sublime; since this skillful means possesses the merit of manifesting the ultimate reality, the compilers of the canon have titled it the "Chapter on Skillful Means."
Second, the name is partial while the meaning is complete.
If one were to designate [the teaching] as "ultimate reality," it would contradict the provisional means.
Now, although the provisional title of this chapter is partial, its actual dharma-body is perfectly complete; thus, it manifests the dual excellence of both the provisional and the ultimate.
Third, the case where both name and substance do not shift.
This consists of four propositions:
first, the name shifts while the substance does not, as in the statement: "Directly abandoning expedient means, he teaches only the unsurpassed path."
Up to the fourth [case], both name and substance do not function; as it is said, "We are now truly śrāvakas.
Because the name does not function, it is titled the "Expedient Means" Chapter.
Fourth, revealing the opening of the provisional and the transcendence of the ultimate.
In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the provisional is opened to reveal the real; outside the provisional, there is no real.
The function of the Dharma is able to penetrate all, and its very essence is secret and wondrous.

If one were to indicate the ultimate reality, it would merely result in a state of mutual dependence; in order to manifest the merit of absolute transcendence, it is titled the "Expedient Means" Chapter.
Fifth, it manifests the teaching that explains delusion.
The Patriarch said:
"Were it not for this present scripture, who would be willing to praise this teaching that explains delusion?
By pointing toward the deluded and defiled mind, it serves as the very means for one's own practice."
Thus we know that this provisional means (*upāya*) possesses great power to clarify delusion.
Sixth, the unity of bestowal and opening:
what was bestowed in the past was precisely the provisional [aspect] of the reality that is bestowed.
What is opened today is the opening of the provisional as being identical to the real; thus one perceives the non-duality between bestowal and opening.
Seventh, distinguishing this from previous sutras:

although the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Sūtra on Requiting Kindness* both establish the name "expedient means," since these are expedients external to the essence, how could they be the same as the "expedient means of identical essence" found in this present chapter?
What has been taught since antiquity does not exceed these seven points.
My former teacher remarked that the detailed exposition of the "Old Commentary" (Jiuguan) had lost the ultimate correctness of the meaning.
Therefore, I have established two principles—Adherence to the Text (*fuwen*) and Investigation of the Intent (*yuanyi*)—to further elucidate the titles of the chapters:
First, regarding the "Appended Text": when the compilers of the sutra establish chapters and append texts, one must distinguish between the general and the specific.

Why is this? The five characters of the primary title generally indicate both the provisional and the ultimate aspects of the Dharma, while the metaphors present both the flower and the fruit together.

Therefore, throughout the three cycles of revelation, the two gates of the original and the trace have been opened; the entire text of this scripture does not depart from the dharma of the provisional and the real.
If this present chapter were to further establish the dual headings of "provisional" and "real," it would be no different from the general title.

2. Regarding the original intent: words exist for the sake of conveying meaning. This sutra reveals the provisional to manifest the ultimate; its underlying intent lies in the provisional. Therefore, it says:

"The Buddhas of the past, by means of countless skillful means, various causes and conditions, and various parables, have expounded all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; these dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle."

Without expedient means (upāya), there is no way to clarify the ultimate reality; therefore, by means of karmic conditions, one uses expedient teachings to awaken others to the truth. Thus it is said: "If one does not point to that which was opened, there is no way to speak of the reality. This detailed exposition of the application of expedients is intended to reveal [the truth].
Therefore, the Master of the Commentary (Ji-zhu) explains that by opening the gate of skillful means, he reveals the true nature, stating:
"To reveal" means to point out; it refers to indicating the place where reality is perceived.
Now, where is this place of perceiving reality?
In the past, there were expedient means that were exclusively provisional;

today, this teaching explains that these expedient means possess the characteristic of reality. Since these are expedient means that are themselves the reality, they differ from the expedient means of former sutras, and thus they receive the name "mysterious and wondrous."
Therefore, the author of the sutra titles this chapter "Expedient Means" (*upāya*).
As soon as one speaks of "expedient means," it is itself the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*).
Thus, Śāriputra raised a doubt, saying:
"Why do you so earnestly praise and extol 'expedient means' (upāya)?
From this, one knows that "expedient means" is truly the general designation for opening the provisional and the great name for manifesting the real!
Alternatively, someone might ask:
"Now, if it is by opening the provisional that one is called 'expedient' (*upāya*), since the *Vimalakīrti* has not yet opened the provisional, how can it be called 'expedient'?
If it is indeed called 'expedient,' why is the provisional not opened?"
Answer: Regarding the term "expedient means" (upāya) mentioned in that sutra, the commentary states:

"This chapter primarily elucidates the assistance rendered in propagating the Buddha's teachings; through skillful and strategic means, it benefits sentient beings according to their capacities, causing them to enter into wisdom and give rise to the spiritual faculties. Therefore, it is called 'expedient means.'"
"Although it is called 'expedient means' (upāya), since the capacity and conditions [of the audience] were present at that very seat, who knows what was realized? That too was an expedient means.
Therefore, in the past, the name "expedient means" did not yet reveal its provisional nature.

Next, regarding the meaning of the chapter title: my ancestor [Master Zhiyi] provided a preliminary commentary on the title, establishing three kinds of skillful means—namely, the application of the Dharma, the capacity for penetration, and the secret mystery. I shall first provide a general overview of these, followed by a detailed explanation.
Furthermore, regarding the general indication: these three skillful means—the first two derive from the ancient teachings, while the last one belongs to the present sutra.
As for the first being named "Dharma-Application" (*dharmaprayoga*), the commentary states:
"'Fang' (方) means 'dharma' (*dharma*)."
"Expedient means" (bian) refers to application.
The Dharma has its squareness and roundness; application has its variations and convergences.
The three provisional means are the carpenter's square and the ruler; the one ultimate reality is the compass and the circle.
The commentary states:

"Initially, the name is established based on the 'ability to employ' the Three Teachings; the Dharma is that which is employed, while the 'employment' is the ability to employ. Although both the Dharma and its employment pertain to all four teachings, there are differences in their respective degrees of squareness or roundness and in how they are reconciled; therefore, the designation 'expedient means' (upāya) is established as a provisional name."

Because provisional means do not immediately coincide with reality, they were distinguished from the former [category] to establish provisional means as being external to the perfected nature; this is not the intended meaning of the present chapter.
Within the text, when "the perfect" (yuan) is cited, it belongs to the true reality (zhenshi), and is mentioned only in contrast [to the provisional].
The second is called "the one who can penetrate. The commentary states:
"Furthermore, 'expedient means' (upāya) refers to a gate.
A gate is named for its ability to penetrate; it penetrates that which is to be penetrated."

Skillful means and provisional strategies are all introductory guides that serve as gateways to the ultimate reality; once the ultimate reality is revealed, its realization is due to the efficacy of these skillful means, which thus derive their name from their capacity to manifest it.
The commentary states:
"Regarding the second interpretation, the provisional is subsumed under the 'ability to penetrate,' and thus the three teachings may also be termed 'expedient means' (upāya).

Although these [teachings] do not immediately constitute the Perfect through their capacity alone, they serve as a remote expression; therefore, the Perfect that is expressed also carries the connotation of the expedient means of the expressive words."
Therefore, it should be known that this is not the intended meaning of the present chapter.
Furthermore, it is said:

"Now, by means of the three [teachings], one is explained; the three serve as the instruments for explaining the one reality. Thus, the three names are the 'explanatory agents' (nengquan). Consequently, the three preceding teachings—along with their doctrines, practitioners, and principles—all function as explanatory agents."
It further states:
"Neither breaking nor immediately [attaining], one enters the ultimate through provisional means; thus, the name 'cultivation' is established.
If prior to this, regarding the two flavors and three teachings, bodhisattvas of sharp faculties may have attained [realization] through manifest revelation."
Regarding the two teachings and the two vehicles, only the secret [teaching] attains it.
Because one enters by means of it, it is called a "gate.
Third, as for the name "Secret and Sublime," the Commentary states:
"Method (fang) refers to the esoteric;
expedient means (bian) refers to the wondrous.
To wondrously penetrate the method is itself the true esoteric."
The priceless jewel within the undergarment is no different from the single jewel upon the king’s head;
the hired laborer is likewise no different from the son of the householder. They are non-dual and indistinguishable.
Such words as these are secret and sublime.
As the sutra says:
"Only I know this mark, and the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise; cease, cease! There is no need to speak, for my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable."
"Therefore, using 'secret' (mi) to explain 'method' (fang) and 'wondrous' (miao) to explain 'expediency' (bian) precisely captures the meaning of this present chapter.
The Record states:
"Only upon reaching the third explanation do the three provisional [means] become one reality."
"This refers to the provisional that points directly to the real; only then can it be called the 'expedient means' of the present sutra.
It further states:
"The third explanation is precisely the intended meaning of this current chapter."
However, regarding the former two interpretations, they were merely termed "partial gates" (piān-mén) in the past and were kept secret without being explained.
Now that these partial gates are opened, they are precisely the locus of the Perfect (yuán); therefore, it is called "secret and subtle" (bìmì).
Because it is manifest and clearly evident, it is called the "True Secret.
Someone asked:
"The *Miaole ji* states:..."
"It is through the provisional that the real functions as the body upon which it relies;
it is through the real that the provisional functions as the body of its own essence.
I do not yet understand whether this third name, "Secret and Sublime," is established based on the body upon which it relies?
"Is it named according to its essential nature?
He replied:

"This is because it is based on its essential nature; that is, the very substance upon which it relies. Therefore, it is said that what was previously secret has now been revealed, and thus becomes 'wondrous' in the present."
It further states:
"The third text also opens up the previous two, such that they are neither the agent nor the object;
furthermore, by means of the capacity to penetrate, both are opened up and established as the object."
"Skillfulness regarding what is appropriate is called 'expedient means' (upāya).
Therefore, wondrous expedient means differs from mere methods and serves as the gateway to penetration.
It further states:
"Therefore, although the perfect [teaching] that transcends partiality also possesses internal expedient means, it is termed 'secret and wondrous' (bi-miao).
While the name 'secret and wondrous' appears similar to that of the third [teaching], its meaning is actually distinct."
Why is this? In the third [period], it is the act of revealing and manifesting that is considered sublime; here, however, it is the unique and perfect [teaching] that is considered sublime.
This distinguishes between the present and the past, as the meanings of "secret" and "sublime" differ.
Reflect deeply upon our Patriarch, who established the three stages of the teaching: if the first two were absent, how could the lotus be manifested?

Thus, the flower is used to employ provisional means; yet if the third stage were lacking, how could the manifestation of the lotus from within the flower—revealing the ultimate reality—be made clear?
The essence pervades a single transformation, while its wondrous manifestations shine forth across the seven volumes.
Were it not for the emergence of the *dhāraṇī*, who could have proclaimed this meaning?
I delve into and look up to its firm loftiness, sighing that words are insufficient to express my admiration.

Next, regarding the specific explanation: if categorized according to the teachings of the various periods, the first two belong to the former teachings; as they employ dharmas that can lead others across, they are all provisional expedients of distinct substance (*bhinna-svabhāva*).
The latter one belongs to the present sutra; as it is a secret and wondrous expedient, it is called a provisional expedient of identical substance (*eka-svabhāva*).
Regarding the determination of the characteristics of this secret and wondrous skillful means for subverting and revealing:
according to the standard instructions of former masters, some determine it to be that which is subverted, while others maintain it to be that which is revealed.
Within one school in India, when discussing the provisional [truth] of the same essence, they determine it to be that which is subverted.
First, according to the metaphor of the opening lotus: the original intent of the Buddha’s appearance in the world was to reveal the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
Because sentient beings were not yet capable of receiving it, he provisionally bestowed the teachings of the past; this is likened to the blossoming of peach and plum flowers.
Upon reaching the *Lotus Sūtra*, as the Dharma is both pure, perfect, and supremely wondrous, it consequently employs the lotus flower to establish three analogies:
first, "the flower for the sake of the lotus," which is a metaphor for establishing provisional means for the sake of the ultimate reality.
Previously, during the four periods, the provisional application of means was not yet taught; this was termed "different substance" (yītǐ).

Now, since the *Anantamukha-sūtra* states, "From the one pure path, there are issued forth two, three, and four," it subsumes the former "different substance" into the present "same substance" (tóngtǐ).
Since provisional means are applied based on reality, they are likened to the flower of the lotus.
Second, as the flower opens and the lotus appears, this opening of the provisional flower of the first phrase reveals the reality of the lotus fruit of the second phrase.
Therefore, within each of the "Chapters on the Five Buddhas," there are two sections: the opening of the provisional (kaiquan) and the revelation of the real (xianshi).
The opening of the provisional consists of the textual narration of past teachings, serving as the basis for the revelation of the real.
Therefore, the "same essence" (*samavajra*) of the *Anantārthasūtra* is that which is sublated by the present *Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra*.
Third, the falling of the petals and the formation of the lotus is a metaphor for the abolition of the provisional and the establishment of the real.
The introductory section (*nidāna*) is entirely discarded as the provisional means toward the ultimate reality; the main body (*samyak-artha*) stands alone as the reality within the provisional.
Next, relying on the principle of the provisional being temporarily employed—the provisional is termed "provisional" because it is temporary and is discarded once its function is fulfilled;
the real is termed "real" because it is a true record, the final destination to which all points lead.
Thus, one knows that all ten provisional designations (*prajñapti*) are thereby refuted.
If mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*) are themselves provisional designations, how could they belong to that which is revealed!
Third, according to the definitive interpretations of the Patriarchs, as stated in the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa):
"Untie the provisional topknot of the same essence and bestow the bright pearl of the true aspect.
Furthermore, the *Yili* states:
"As cited from the *Lotus Sūtra*, the body of this scripture is solely the One Reality."
The preface to the *Wen xu* (Preface to the Text) takes the teachings of the past as that which is opened [by the present].
Since it states that the divisions are ultimately one reality, the provisional that shares the same essence is what is to be sublated. Furthermore, recent scholars have claimed:

"While there is opening from the perspective of names, there is no opening from the perspective of meaning; for example, the Perfect Teaching sublates ignorance as being identical to the dharma-nature, and this chapter likewise opens the provisional as being identical to the real."

I observe that the former masters who refuted the provisional [teaching] as being of the same essence erred in two ways: first, in their formulation of metaphors; second, in their failure to understand the opening of the provisional.
First, regarding the error in formulating metaphors: the flower exists for the sake of the lotus.
As the Great Master said:
"For the sake of the ten subtleties, the ten coarsenesses are opened out.
This is like flowers blooming for the sake of the lotus; regarding the essence of the Dharma, their functioning in the past all belonged to the category of coarse phenomena.
Why is it that all are considered "flowers for the sake of the lotus"?
Since both are metaphors for the Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*), seeing them merely as comparable objects results in a confused analogy.

Furthermore, regarding the principle of "bestowing the provisional based on the real" (*shi shi shi quan*): from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* through to the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*, all [teachings] distinguish the three truths separately; these all serve as the "real" for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, while the provisional teachings of the four periods and three vehicles are bestowed. Therefore, this is termed "bestowing the provisional based on the real."

If one were to use this single phrase alone as an analogy for the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, it would merely manifest that which is being illustrated, while the Dharma itself remains deficient.

Second, regarding the obscuration of the provisional (*upāya*): throughout the four periods and three teachings, the essence [of the Buddha-nature] was externalized for the sake of transforming others; because the capacities of sentient beings had not yet reached full maturity, the provisional was concealed and the real was spoken of. Therefore, these are not ultimate and belong to the coarse category of "different essence" (*bhinnasvabhāva*).

Only now, pointing back to the past, do we realize that what was previously held was not truly real; once the biased attachments to the teachings have been dispelled, one immediately knows that the essence itself is fundamentally wondrous.
This method for transforming others is entirely the provisional skillful means of one’s own practice.
The non-duality of the provisional and the real is what is called "identical essence.
Therefore, the Patriarch said:
"Once the real has been revealed, the provisional is entirely the real; one must not say that the provisional is not ultimate."
How much more so when the Patriarch said:
"Who would be willing to take this tainted, outflowing consciousness of the triple world and have it praised by the Buddha?
Since it is praised by the Buddha, how could it not be that which is manifested?"

Next, regarding that which is revealed by this definitive [teaching]: the single school of the Southern Screen (Nanping) all maintains that although the World-Honored One turned the wheel of Dharma over a long period in the past, the capacities of those to be converted were diverse, and thus the teachings he bestowed were not uniform.
Although the three teachings were expounded, it was not said that these were provisional means identical with the real;
although the Perfect Vehicle was performed, it was not yet declared that this was the real identical with the provisional.

Since the provisional and the real each accommodated their respective audiences and the Great and Small vehicles remained separated, the former teachings are termed "provisional in essence" (yiti-quan).

Later, at Vulture Peak, he proclaimed the wondrous *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, revealing the previously hidden and secret Dharma as the subtle and profound teaching of the present; because the provisional and the real are perfectly integrated, they are said to be of the same essence.
Since the dharmas are such that their coarse and subtle aspects are mutually identical, the Buddha’s transformation is perfected in both phenomenon and principle.
If they are taken as that which is to be refuted, it serves to reveal the subtle.
Thus, the commentary states:
"The third interpretation clarifies the preceding two: that which is neither the agent nor the object, as well as the capacity for penetration, are both clarified and established as the object.
This can be taken as proof that the secret and wondrous is not something to be opened!"
Regarding the three analogies of the lotus flower, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) and other texts record five masters who provide differing interpretations:
the first says that there is a distinction between the opposing treatise and one's own treatise.
If we consider the contrast between the partial and the perfect, those of different substance are what is to be destroyed, while those of identical substance are what is to be revealed.
This is illustrated by the fact that in the three [lower] teachings, the three delusions must be severed, whereas in the Perfect Teaching, the three delusions are not severed.
According to the Perfect Teaching itself, forty-two grades [of delusion] must be severed;
therefore, even the provisional [teachings] of the same essence belong to that which is to be subverted.

Now, if one were to discuss the partial and the perfect in contrast, the first three [teachings] would be designated as provisional while the Perfect Teaching belongs to the real—how then could they be discussed in contrast?
But if you claim that the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) is already designated as "expedient means of the same substance" (tongti quan) and thus need not be sublated,

then why now— when revealing the Real by opening up the Expedient (kaiquan xianshi), where opening up the partial is precisely the Perfect— is it instead argued, using the three analogies of the lotus, that this is merely the internal discourse of the Perfect Teaching itself, which sublates the expedient means of the same substance, yet fails to demonstrate the power of the present sutra to open up the expedient means at all?
Second, it is said that the sentient capacity and the Buddha’s intent differ.
While the sentient capacity may manifest as distinct entities, the Buddha’s intent is of a single essence (*samatā*).
Now, I say that while such exalted expressions may be unique to this present sutra, the Buddha’s intent is not restricted to this alone.

Based on this ancestral intent, although the revelation of the teaching according to the capacities of beings is restricted to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the original secret intention of the Buddha pervades all four periods.
Thus, both the dispositions of sentient beings and the intention of the Buddha are primarily concerned with the teachings of the past.

If one relies on past interpretations to judge the present sutra, it is like wishing to reach Hunan while traveling northward across the Great Wall; though one’s intention may be earnest, the path becomes ever more distant.
Third, it is said that the Dharma is inherently sublime, while coarseness arises from the dispositions of sentient beings.

Although provisional teachings of distinct entities are established, in reality the essence of the Dharma is fundamentally subtle and wondrous; this is precisely what constitutes the "identical essence" (tongti).
Now, it is said as the Master of Records stated:
"Simply open its emotional state, and the principle will naturally return to its source.
He further stated:
"What is it that is opened?
It is precisely that which covers.
Since one has merely destroyed the deluded state of the covering, how could one ever have opened the phenomena that were the object of confusion?

The fourth point concludes the explanation regarding the opening [of the provisional]. Since the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) explains the "provisional topknot of the same essence" (*tongti-quanji*), having already pointed to the sutras of the Trace Gate that circulate, this section concludes by showing how the distinct essences (*yiti*) have been opened to become the same essence (*tongti*).
Now, regarding the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct" (Anlehangpin): although its text appears later, its metaphor actually clarifies what precedes it.
To claim that it specifically characterizes the orthodox teaching and reveals the subtle by opening up the coarse is a statement devoid of meaning; it is nothing more than empty talk.
To say that "the five clouds share the same substance" as that which is to be opened [revealed] implies that those of different substances are likewise indestructible.
This statement is reckless; I am struck with terror by its words, for they are as boundless as the Milky Way.

Now, examining the ancients, it is because they were ignorant of the textual meanings of the various sections of the Mountain School (Shan-jia) that their treatises on the revelation of the provisional (kaiquan) were verbose yet lacked substance.
I shall now arrange these texts side by side so that [the confusion] may be dissolved like ice melting and frost thawing, such that diverse paths lead to the same destination.

First, the metaphor is explained. The traditional interpretation of the lotus flower is that it may exclusively represent the sublime, or it may simultaneously be compared to coarse flowers when contrasted with them; in such a comparison, the lotus is sublime in both respects.
Within the lotus itself, the flower is likewise both sublime and coarse.
Now, since what is illustrated (the *dharma*) possesses both the provisional and the real, it is revealed that the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) likewise encompasses both the coarse and the subtle.
We shall first distinguish between the provisional and the real of that which is illustrated, and subsequently analyze the coarse and the subtle of the illustration itself.
As for the actual meaning of the distribution of power (*bunken*), it summarizes the essential points and comprises five major themes:
first, cause and effect; second, nine and one; third, the present and the past; fourth, the real and the conventional; and fifth, the fundamental and the manifested.
First, regarding the division into cause and fruit:
among the ten realms, the first seven are thus categorized as causes and are provisional;
the latter two, being the retributive fruits, are real.
Second, the provisional and the real are partially distinguished within the nine [realms]. The *Miaoxuan* states:
"The remaining flowers are coarse; they metaphorically represent the causes and effects of the ten 'thusnesses' across the nine dharma-realms."
This exquisite flower serves as a metaphor for the ten aspects of the cause and effect within the Buddha’s Dharma-realm.
Third, regarding the distinction between the ancient and the present:
the past is regarded as provisional, while the present is taken as the ultimate reality.
Therefore, the *Myōhon* (Miaoxuan) says:
"The single lotus causes the flowers to bloom; this is a metaphor for establishing provisional means for the sake of the ultimate reality.
Although various paths are taught, their true purpose is the Buddha Vehicle."
Fourth, regarding the distinction between the ultimate and the conventional:

the wisdom that perceives emptiness illuminates the ultimate and is thus the real; the wisdom that perceives the conventional illuminates the conventional and is thus the provisional; the middle wisdom that illuminates both is both provisional and real; and the middle way that transcends both is neither provisional nor real.
Therefore, the *Myōraku-ki* states:
"Because it is contrasted with the past, four propositions must be established.

While this general outline of the Dharma-characteristics is thus, when specifically discussing the present chapter, it pertains only to the third [proposition]; furthermore, as it constitutes half of the provisional teaching, it is titled the 'Chapter on Expedient Means' (*Upāya-parivarta*)."
5. Regarding the distinction between the Original and the Traced (honji-suijaku):
As stated in my own preface, "The remote and eternal original fruition is indicated and metaphorically represented by the lotus."
"The perfect path of non-duality is illustrated by means of the flower.
Although the provisional and the real encompass five meanings, here we discuss the revelation of the provisional solely in terms of the realms, the schools, and the teachings.
Next, to clarify the coarse and subtle aspects of the analogy, the *Xuan Yi* (Profound Meaning) preface speaks of the lotus flower:
first, "the flower for the sake of the lotus" is an analogy for establishing the provisional through the real;
second, "the blooming of the flower" is an analogy for opening the provisional, while "the appearance of the lotus" is an analogy for revealing the real.
Third, the falling of the petals is a metaphor for the relinquishing of the provisional, while the formation of the lotus is a metaphor for the establishment of the real.
One should proceed through these three analogies, drawing them out and extending their application.
Furthermore, as for the metaphor of the lotus flower, it was first proclaimed in this present sutra to illustrate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (the Wondrous Dharma).

The person of the Perfect Teaching (yuanren) practices the three contemplations within a single mind (yixin san guan) all at once; upon ascending to the stages (zhù) and entering the reality (shí), they take this as their purity.
The *Miaozong* says:
“If one discusses actual realization, in this land there is only the dwelling place of those who are sages of the Perfect Teaching.”

In the case of others at the first stage (*bhūmi*), their realization is identical to that of the Perfect [Teaching]; as they receive retribution according to reality, how could there be any difference in quality or degree?

However, regarding the path of the teachings (*śāsana-mārga*), because the ten stages are not yet fused, the land they perceive as a result of their retribution differs from that of those of the Perfect Teaching.

The *Zabian* (Miscellaneous Compilation) takes both together, meaning that for those who achieve [enlightenment] through partiality rather than entering gradually or all at once, there are the two types of contemplation—skillful and unskillful—cultivated in the Separate and Perfect Teachings;
as for "true recompense" and "purity or impurity," these refer to the two aspects of fusion and obstruction perceived by those dwelling on the stages.

This is because individuals who have long practiced the gradual path, even though they have turned toward and cultivated the perfect [teaching], still perceive a portion of defiled and obstructive form at the time of entering the stages; this is termed "impurity."

The person of the Perfect Teaching (yuanren) practices only sudden cultivation from beginning to end; at the moment of entering and abiding [in the stages], they perceive only the signs of the interpenetration of this land, which is termed "pure.
The *Wangsheng ji* (Record of Rebirth) refutes the teachings of the Provisional and Distinct Teachings, yet its own account of perceiving divine wisdom contradicts the *Fuxing*.
Those who study the Dharma through its principles should reflect with careful scrutiny upon the ultimate realization of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*,
which encompasses both the pure and impure realms of *śāntaprabhāsa*.
As the *Miaozongchao* states:
"If one speaks of the tranquil light (jìguāng) with respect to others who equally realize the perfect reality, it refers solely to the true cause;

Now, discussing the path of teaching, it is said that when the ultimate fruit is realized, one merely severs twelve grades of ignorance, and even the Land of Quiescent Light remains defiled.
Perfect knowledge must sever forty-two grades of ignorance to be called ultimately pure.
The *Record of Rebirth* states:

"Now, in relation to the contrast between partial and complete realization, the middle and lower grades are combined and termed 'partial realization'; thus, the Land of Peaceful Light remains defiled."
When wondrous enlightenment reaches its highest grade and true permanence is fully perfected, it is then called ultimate purity.
Please observe the present text: the dwelling places where all Buddhas and Tathāgatas roam and reside are the most supremely pure lands.

This is correctly based on the true cause and ultimate fruit of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*), in contrast to which the pure and impure are partially distinguished. Siming said:

The *Kanzhengji* states: "Only by means of the partial realization of the *śānta-prabhāsvara-loka* (the world of tranquil light) does one subsequently arise in the *bhūta-vipāka* (the realm of true retribution)."
"Now, with respect to partial realization, one still retains ignorance; because of this ignorance, it is defiled.
Because ultimate ignorance has been exhausted, it is pure.
The *Zabian* raises an objection, saying:
"If that were so, then the defiled would constitute the realm of actual retribution, and the pure would constitute the realm of tranquil light.
Now, it is said that because the divisions of ignorance are shattered and a small portion of the signless is realized, it is 'defiled'."
Because ignorance is completely exhausted and one realizes ultimate signlessness, it is "pure.
Regarding the essence of the four concentrations (*dhyāna*), former masters generally take the three paths as the essence of the essence for the three lower lands.
Quoting the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), it says:
"The three paths of the segmented [rebirth] refer to the afflictions of views and thought, which constitute the path of affliction (*kleśa-mārga*).
Afflictions moisten karma, which constitutes the path of karma (*karma-mārga*)."
The arising within the realm of sensation constitutes the path of suffering.
Regarding the three paths of expedient means: the myriad dust-like delusions are called the path of afflictions;
untainted karma is termed the path of karma; [and the resulting rebirth is the path of suffering].
The birth and death of transformation is called the path of suffering.
The three paths of the true retribution refer to ignorance and delusion as the path of afflictions;
non-outflow and non-non-outflow karma as the path of action; and [the resulting states] as the path of suffering.
The transformation of that land is termed the Path of Suffering.
It universally takes the three virtues as its underlying substance.
Thus, the Path of Suffering is the Dharmakāya; karmic bondage is liberation; and afflictions are bodhi.
The former master stated that delusion and karma are the cause, while the path of suffering is the fruit.

Within the present "substance of land" (*dharmadhātu*), among the three worlds, we take only the path of suffering as the fundamental substance of the thousandfold lands, and further take the three virtues as its supporting substance.
Therefore, Jingxi said:

"Principle has no fixed location; it is omnipresent within phenomena. Thus, the three lands are taken as its substratum.
Master Guangci, following the *Myōryaku*, states:
"The four virtues of the original nature serve as the substratum, while the four virtues of cultivated virtue serve as that which relies upon them."
He then pointed to the three causes of cultivated virtue as the essential substance and the three dharmas of inherent virtue as the basis.

Fifth, the "Manifestation of Characteristics": this refers to the teaching gate that reveals the characteristics of the four lands.
First, the characteristics of identity and difference are shown:
the Sahā world and the Land of Ultimate Bliss are distinct in their impurity and purity, and are thus called "different";

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states:

Third, the characteristics of the horizontal and vertical are shown.
Previous explanations of the horizontal and vertical were confused and disordered in their phrasing and meaning, thereby bewildering students.
Now, these two meanings are divided for clarity; thus they are easily understood.
First, regarding the classification of the lands, as stated in the *Myōhon* (The Profound Meaning):
"If one distinguishes them, it is said that the land of expedient means (*upāya*) is outside the triple world;
if one distinguishes them, it is said that the land of true retribution (*bhūtadharma-vipāka*) is outside the land of expedient means."
According to this analysis, it is said that the Land of Peaceful Light (Jiguang) exists outside the Land of Real Reward (Shibao).
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* asks:
"Beyond the three lands, how does [the Pure Land] differ from empty space?"
The answer is:
"They are identical in principle yet distinct in manifestation.
To speak of their distinction in manifestation: the Dharma-body is itself the land."
Apart from the body there is no land; apart from the land there is no body.
It is merely the true suchness and the reality-mark, which is neither wisdom nor an object, yet is spoken of as wisdom and as an object;
it is neither body nor land, yet is spoken of as body and as land.
"Based on this analysis, the meaning should be understood as vertical (sequential).
If one relies on the principle of mutual identity (*xiāngjí*), as the *Miaole* says:

"It is not that apart from the Land of Tranquil Light (Sukhāvatī), there exists a separate Sahā world.

"As for 'horizontal understanding,' it is as previously cited from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: one perceives the [upper] two lands within this very land."
"Therefore, though he was briefly rebuked, seeing the pure [land], he was not startled; that he pressed the earth with his toe is precisely what this refers to.
Based on this mutual identity (*sō-soku*), the meaning belongs to the horizontal dimension (*gyō*).
Regarding the inclusion by way of characteristics, the *Vimalakīrti-ṭīkā* states:
"Since one land encompasses all lands, by attaining this realm, it universally includes the two lower realms."
"Applying this principle, the superior encompasses the inferior; thus, the lands are also categorized horizontally.
Second, regarding the division according to the teachings, the *Miaole ji* states:
"Discussing the substance of the lands horizontally, they correspond to the teachings."
"Regarding the vertical discourse on the lands, it concerns the extent of the application of the teachings.
As for this vertical discourse, the *Mohe Zhiguan* states:
"If one correlates the Four Noble Truths vertically with the various lands, there are instances of increase and decrease."
"There are four [levels of] co-residence: three are provisional expedients, two are of true retribution, and the Land of Tranquil Light is but one.
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explains: "Vertically, this is established in accordance with the teachings set forth to correspond to the capacities of sentient beings."
Since the capacities [of sentient beings] differ according to increase or decrease, the teachings consequently exhibit distinctions.
Because the four lands are contrasted with these teachings in terms of their relative superiority and inferiority, as well as their extent, they are termed "vertical.
Thus, while the characteristics of the lands are vertical, the teachings themselves are explained horizontally.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-ṭīkā* states:
"However, speaking in terms of the horizontal [classification], the Shared Residence (tongju) possesses all four [levels].
In the remaining three, these gradually diminish; the Shared Residence has a diverse range of spiritual capacities (*indriya*)."
He consequently established the four teachings as skillful means, yet he instructed them solely through the Mahāyāna, with the principle being exclusively the Separate and Perfect [teachings].

This was because those who had received the Tripiṭaka were merely beginners in these skillful means and had not yet practiced the Shared gate; thus, he taught them so that they might come to understand.

He then discussed the Shared Teaching (Samvṛti-yāna) to sweep away attachments; regarding the Reward Land (vipākaphala), it is based on practice, while the realization of the Way is identical to the Perfect [Teaching].
However, when employing the teaching according to the stage of "having remainder," the pedagogical path transforms the capacities of beings by explaining the Distinct as different from the Perfect.
Only by employing both teachings can one give rise to the fruition of true recompense (shibao).

Since the superior grade of the Land of Quiescent Light (jiguang) does not require the employment of teachings—being intended only for those of middle and lower capacities—the Perfect Vehicle (yuan-sheng) exists.
Although the characteristics of the established teachings are horizontal, they become vertical when categorized according to the distinct divisions of the lands (*bhūmi*).

If one considers their mutual identity (*samasamavartin*), the *tongju* (shared residence) land horizontally possesses the essence and characteristics of the four lands, which corresponds to the purport of the Four Teachings.
The Tripitaka teachings discuss arising and ceasing, which corresponds to the stage of abiding together with the unconditioned;
the Shared Teaching discusses illusory transformations as being identical to emptiness, which corresponds to the stage of realizing the truth through skillful means;
the Distinct Teaching receives its name from its engagement with phenomena, which corresponds to the stage of experiencing the fruition in the Land of Real Reward.
The Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) speaks of inherent virtues (xingde), which correspond to the ontological essence of the Dharma-realm of Quiescent Light (jiguang).
When these are compared horizontally across the four teachings, there is no longer any distinction of superiority or inferiority; therefore, it is called "horizontal" (heng).
Regarding the fourth point, "manifesting the marks of existence and non-existence," the *Miaozong* states:

"When the sutras and treatises speak of the 'markless' (*animitta*) Dharma-realm of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsvara*), this refers to the complete exhaustion of all defiled and obstructive marks; it does not mean that it is like empty space where nothing exists. This is because when the three delusions are ultimately purified, the form and mind of both the environment and its inhabitants become ultimately manifest."
Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
"By the cessation of this form, one attains eternal form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise."
The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* refers to these as the five aggregates of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), which is also what the *Lotus Sūtra* calls the permanence of worldly phenomena.

In the *Large Perfection of Wisdom*, form and fragrance are none other than the Middle Way; this is precisely what is called the ultimate Land of Bliss, the ultimate gold and jewels, the ultimate lotus pond, and the ultimate jade tree.
Furthermore, this [teaching] exhausts the abandonment of defilement and reaches the ultimate source of the attainment of purity.

Therefore, realms such as the domain of suffering are categorized as belonging to the three obstacles, while the golden treasures of the Land of Bliss are taken as the *Sukhāvatī* (the Land of Quiescent Light).
If one speaks in terms of the equality of purity and defilement, then the ultimate mire and silt of the realm of suffering is taken as the Land of Peaceful Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*).
These two explanations merely accord with the *siddhānta* (the established tenets); there is nothing in them that is not perfectly complete.

Since even "one" does not exist, how could there be such characteristics as suffering, pleasure, flowers, or a womb?

"Non-characteristic is non-characterizing; that is to say, it is without the characteristic of birth-and-death and without the characteristic of nirvana.

Speaking of this in terms of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), pure awakening (*viśuddha-bodhi*) accords with the meaning of conceptualization.

Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-vyākhyāna* states: "Question:

by means of the empty space, he symbolized the inherent virtues of the supported.
How can one accept only that which is expressed by the "cultivated nature" (xiuxing) as taught by Śākyamuni, while completely discarding the "expressing medium" of body and land?

Furthermore, since the two—cultivation and nature—are not identical, others take the principle of the nature-endowment (*xingde*) as the supported and the wisdom of original enlightenment (*benjue*) as the supporter; they take the principle of cultivated virtue (*xiude*) as the supported and the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*shijue*) as the supporter.
The principle of cultivating virtue is that which is depended upon, while the wisdom of initial awakening is that which depends [upon it].

Now, when fundamental awakening is considered in relation to cultivation, both belong to the nature (*prakṛti*); when the practice of cultivation is considered in relation to the nature, both belong to cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
According to their understanding, they establish a view in which nature subsumes nature and cultivation accords with cultivation; this is not the non-duality of cultivation and nature.

It should rather be said that "cultivation arises entirely from nature. Therefore, the land upon which one relies is identical to the body that relies upon it, and quiescent radiance is the response-body (nirmāṇakāya).

Since all cultivation resides within the nature, the body that serves as the support is itself the land that is supported; thus, the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*).
Only then is the equality of body and land revealed, whereby one perceives the non-differentiation between phenomena and principle.
Furthermore, it is said:
"If one claims that the serene light (sìguāng) is signless (wúxiàng), then it would be identical to the partial truth (piānzhēn), just like the great void.
This arises from not understanding the distinction between the two principles of the Great and Small Vehicles, and the difference between wisdom and non-wisdom.
As the *Vimalakīrti Commentary* states:
"The dharma-nature of the Mahāyāna is precisely the nature of true quiescent wisdom; it is not the same as the principle of partial truth found in the Two Vehicles."
Now I ask:
since both the Dharma-body of Quiescent Light and [the realm of] formlessness are devoid of characteristics, upon what dharma does the nature of true quiescent wisdom rely?
Since it is revealed that the nature of wisdom has no basis, this demonstrates that it is not something clearly discerned by superficial consciousness.
The *Zabian* further states:
"If one relies on the mutual identity of the three bodies and the mutual inclusion of the four lands, it must be that each body is identical with the three [bodies] and each land includes all four."
"If this is so, how could the Dharma-body and the land of quiescence be without marks?
Tong replied:

"I shall now discuss for you the principle of the mutual inclusion of the four lands. If we discuss mutual inclusion by correlating phenomena with principle, then the land of quiescence includes the other three lands; this is the whole substance giving rise to its function—being without marks yet possessing marks."
The three lands are fully endowed with quiescence; thus, they entirely employ this essence, wherein appearance is itself non-appearance.
Now I ask:
if they entirely employ this essence, one may attain non-appearance; [but how can there be non-appearance when there are distinct lands?]
When the whole body gives rise to its function, it should be said to possess form;
how can one speak of it as being universally without form?
Furthermore, the *Zabian* says:
Question:
"If the three marks cannot be conflated, why does Jingxi raise the objection:
'Why [refer to] every single dust-mote world-system as being all world-systems?'"
Answer: "This refers to the fact that the nature of the lands (kṣetra) universally encompasses all; therefore, it is called 'all.
This is like the meaning of 'the narrow being universal' in the *Jinbi*."
How can that which is narrow be all-pervasive?
Because the narrow is itself its nature.
It is also like a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru.
"How can a mustard seed contain it?
For the mustard seed is also of the nature [of reality].
This passage only shows that phenomena are themselves the principle; it does not show that the principle is itself phenomena.

If principle were not identical with phenomena, how could a mustard seed contain Mount Sumeru? How could one harm trees while swallowing the great ocean with a single hair, without disturbing the dragons and fish?
The *Zabian* further states:
"If there were no marks of the environment and its inhabitants, then principle would have nothing to manifest and phenomena would have nothing to exist."
"How can it be that the Dharma-body is the same as being extinguished like ashes?
Answer:
"In the Small Vehicle, there is no mark (animitta), which is like the great void; therein lies the principle of the non-arising of dharmas."
The signlessness of the Mahāyāna is like a clear mirror, possessing the nature that manifests images.
Images arise through the confrontation with forms; the mirror itself does not differentiate.
One should not say that because the mirror possesses the nature of manifesting images, its nature is already differentiated.
Now it is said: if one claims that only the nature (xing) is possessed while the characteristics (xiang) are not, how can the *Guanyin xuanyi* state:
"The thousandfold natures and characteristics lie hidden and dormant within the mind"?
Furthermore, the *Fumen* (Gate of Non-duality) states:

"The principle is itself the names and words; within the stage of contemplative practice, there already exists the aspect of the non-duality between the Dharma-body and its physical manifestation. Alas!

Although Xiachuan paid close attention to the teachings of the Mountain School, he merely understood the mutual dependence of cultivation and nature; he did not reach the point where phenomena and principle are fused and identical.
By teaching in violation of the Dharma to his disciples, his lineage has been severed!
Regarding the "six pairs" concerning the body, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra-vyākhyā* states:
"The former two are the Responsive [Buddhas], that is, the abodes of the Responsive Buddhas.
This is because they were born in royal palaces and entered parinirvāṇa beneath the śāla trees; they manifest the signs of birth and death and preach the Dharma of the Tripiṭaka."
The transformation body that dwells together with beings in this world is called the inferior response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇakāya*).
Reaching the lands of further excellence, it manifests as the dharma-nature body (*dharmatākāya*).
When the capacity of sentient beings arises, the response arises; when the capacity ceases, the response ceases.

This differs from the Sahā world; it is common to all Buddhas who have severed their defilements. Since it is not a karmic retribution, it is merely termed a "superior response" (victorious response-body).
The third [land] is both retribution and response, being the dwelling place of the retribution Buddha.

Because it is experienced through the enjoyment for others (*parasaṃbhoga*) and is a retribution corresponding to reality, it accords with the great capacities of Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages; therefore, the Buddha of that land is also called "the Responsive" (*nirmāṇa*).
The latter one [the *dharmakāya*] is merely true purity; it is neither responsive nor retributive, being the abode of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
This refers to the substance of the land, which horizontally corresponds to the four Buddhas.

If one discusses the land vertically, it is a realm where ordinary beings and sages dwell together; therein all four bodies are fully manifested. Because the expedient [body] is exclusively superior, there is no inferior response-body.

In fact, in the Land of Recompense, there are no followers of the Two Vehicles; there are only Buddhas of the Separate and Perfect Teachings. In the Land of Tranquil Light, there is no capacity for [lesser] faculties, and it is solely the wondrous Dharma-body.
Regarding those who misunderstand this: some say that the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states, "If you wish to attain a pure land, you should purify your own mind."
"According as one's mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure.
The mind is like a form or a sound, while the land is like a shadow or an echo; one need only purify one's own mind—why rely on seeking a pure land elsewhere?
Answer:
"Regarding the initial statement 'purity of mind,' one should distinguish between the purity of principle and the purity of phenomena.
First is the purity of nature; second is the purity of phenomena."
Furthermore, regarding the purity of nature, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"The mind-nature of all sentient beings is fundamentally pure.
Because the mind is fundamentally pure, the various fetters of affliction cannot defile or adhere to it, just like empty space."
"Thus, the realms of sentient beings and their lands share the same dharma-nature; even the hells and celestial palaces are all pure lands.
Regarding the purity of these two matters: although their nature is fundamentally pure, the mind has suddenly become deluded."
A single moment of non-awakening allows the two obstacles to obscure one for a long time; one should therefore cultivate the three contemplations to shatter the three delusions.
Thus, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states:
"The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood abide in retributive fruits; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land."
"Only upon ascending to the fruit of wondrous enlightenment does one finally reach ultimate purity.
As for the most base of ordinary beings, be careful not to overstep your station through presumption.
Next, regarding the purity of the land, one must understand its difficulties and ease."
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"In this world, there are two ways of practicing the Path:

the first is the difficult practice, which occurs in the five turbidities of a degenerate age; to seek *avaivartika* [non-retrogression] during the time of immeasurable Buddhas is extremely difficult to attain."
These difficulties are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and cannot be fully described; the *Ten Doubts Treatise* clarifies five kinds of such difficulties. Second is the Easy Path:

this refers to believing the Buddha’s words, being taught the *nien-fo samādhi*, and vowing to be born in the Pure Land. Being sustained by the power of Amitābha Buddha’s vows, one will certainly attain rebirth; this is called the Easy Path.
These seven thematic gates distinguish the various Buddha-lands; though their vertical numbers exceed the dust motes of the earth, they all share the same principle as reflections in a mirror.
While they are unfolded, ten thousand transformations are laid out in profusion; yet when rolled up, not even a single dharma is established.

Furthermore, regarding the additional *wajiten* (Japanese-style diacritics) included here, these marks are not uniform; they have been transcribed after collating them against various scholarly traditions.
